course.title: How Government Works
course.description: What a state is, why people obey one, and how governments are built, compared across the UK, the US, Australia, Germany, India and non-democracies. Each lesson practises one skill on real material: classifying a regime, reading a constitution, seeing who gains from an electoral system, weighing a philosopher's argument, judging what a court can do, and reading regime and turnout data.
course.audience: A curious adult who follows the news and wants to understand how governments differ and why. They know that some countries have presidents and others prime ministers, but have not read Hobbes or Madison, a constitution, or a table of seats and votes. No earlier course is needed.

paragraphs: What a state is, why people obey one, and how governments are built, compared across the UK, the US, Australia, Germany, India and non-democracies. Each lesson practises one skill on real material: classifying a regime, reading a constitution, seeing who gains from an electoral system, weighing a philosopher's argument, judging what a court can do, and reading regime and turnout data.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a described state's claim to obedience rests on (security, consent, custom, a leader, lawful procedure), and apply Locke's test of broken trust to a described government.
You'll be able to classify a described regime by who rules and whose good it serves, and by the four categories of the Regimes of the World data.
You'll be able to read a regime, turnout or population table with its definition in hand, and say what it can and cannot show.
You'll be able to tell from a constitution's text which body holds a power and what checks it, in the United States text of 1787 and the Australian text of 1900.
You'll be able to classify a system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed.
You'll be able to say what a court can and cannot do about a statute in three different systems.
introduction.prerequisites: No earlier Discere course is needed.

modules.title: The state, obedience and regimes
modules.description: Why anyone obeys a state, Aristotle's two questions and the modern categories from democracy to closed autocracy, and how to read the data that sorts countries into them.

modules.title: Constitutions, branches and courts
modules.description: Montesquieu's three powers, which body holds a power in the American and Australian texts, how executives are chosen and removed, and what courts can do.

modules.title: Votes, parties and policy
modules.description: How votes become seats under real formulas, how Madison thought about faction, and how opinion becomes a policy and a budget.

modules.title: Rights, levels of government and the wider world
modules.description: Mill and Tocqueville on the majority, who holds a power in a federation, and how states relate when no one governs them all.

concepts.title: State
concepts.summary: Weber's definition: a compulsory political organisation whose centralised government successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of force within a territory.

concepts.title: Failed state
concepts.summary: A state whose claimed sovereignty over its territory has collapsed or never worked.

concepts.title: Legitimacy
concepts.summary: The right of an authority to rule, as accepted by those it rules.

concepts.title: Foundational and contingent legitimacy
concepts.summary: Mittiga's two parts: ability to ensure safety and security, and exercising power in acceptable ways.

concepts.title: Consent and trust
concepts.summary: Locke: nobody comes under political power without consent, and the people lend power to a government to be used for the ends for which it was lent.

concepts.title: Traditional, charismatic and rational-legal legitimacy
concepts.summary: Weber's three bases of a claim to rule: custom, a leader's personal qualities, and lawful procedure.

concepts.title: Aristotle's six forms
concepts.summary: Rule by one, few or many, for the common good (kingdom, aristocracy, and what Jowett calls a state) or for the rulers' own good (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).

concepts.title: Closed autocracy
concepts.summary: A regime in which citizens cannot choose the chief executive or the legislature through multi-party elections.

concepts.title: Electoral autocracy
concepts.summary: A regime with multi-party elections that lacks the freedoms, such as association and expression, that make them meaningful, free and fair.

concepts.title: Electoral democracy
concepts.summary: A regime with meaningful, free and fair multi-party elections.

concepts.title: Liberal democracy
concepts.summary: An electoral democracy that also protects individual and minority rights, equality before the law, and constrains the executive through the legislature and courts.

concepts.title: Hybrid regime
concepts.summary: A regime combining democratic and autocratic features.

concepts.title: Coded series
concepts.summary: A series in which experts assign each country-year a category against written definitions, so a change in category is a judgement about a defining feature.

concepts.title: Count and share
concepts.summary: A count says how many; a share divides it by a total. A count can rise while a share falls.

concepts.title: Denominator
concepts.summary: What a percentage is a percentage of; turnout here is a share of registered voters, not of adults.

concepts.title: Gap in a series
concepts.summary: A year or country with no row, which says nothing by itself about what happened.

concepts.title: Anomaly
concepts.summary: A value, or a run of identical values, that is unlikely enough to need checking before it is used.

concepts.title: Legislative, executive and judiciary power
concepts.summary: Montesquieu's three: making and repealing laws; making peace or war, embassies and security; punishing crimes and settling disputes between individuals.

concepts.title: Separation of powers
concepts.summary: The principle that these powers be held by different persons or bodies.

concepts.title: Checks and balances
concepts.summary: Constitutional means by which each branch can limit the others, such as a veto.

concepts.title: Fusion of powers
concepts.summary: A system in which executive and legislature are joined, as in the Westminster parliamentary systems.

concepts.title: Union of the three powers
concepts.summary: Montesquieu's example is the Sultan in Turkey, where all three are united in one person.

concepts.title: Vested power
concepts.summary: The word both texts use to say where a power rests: legislative power 'vested in' Congress, executive power 'vested in' a President or the Queen.

concepts.title: Advice and consent
concepts.summary: The Senate's part in treaties and appointments in the American text: the President acts with its agreement.

concepts.title: Appropriation
concepts.summary: A law that authorises money to be drawn from the treasury; both texts say no money may be drawn without one.

concepts.title: Impeachment
concepts.summary: Removal from office on conviction of treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors; the House accuses and the Senate tries.

concepts.title: Text and practice
concepts.summary: A constitution's words and the way it is worked can differ; the Australian text never mentions a Prime Minister or Cabinet.

concepts.title: Confidence
concepts.summary: The support of a majority of parliament on which a parliamentary head of government depends; losing a vote of no confidence ends it.

concepts.title: Presidential system
concepts.summary: A head of government elected separately from the legislature and not removable by it except in extraordinary cases.

concepts.title: Semi-presidential system
concepts.summary: A president alongside a prime minister and cabinet who answer to the legislature.

concepts.title: Cohabitation
concepts.summary: In a semi-presidential system, a president and prime minister from different parties.

concepts.title: Dualism
concepts.summary: A rule that members of parliament resign their seats on becoming ministers, as in the Netherlands, Slovakia and Sweden.

concepts.title: Judicial review
concepts.summary: A court's assessment of whether an action of the executive or, in some systems, a statute is lawful or constitutional.

concepts.title: Declaration of incompatibility
concepts.summary: In the UK, a court's finding that an Act conflicts with the Human Rights Act's rights; it does not disapply the Act and asks Parliament to act.

concepts.title: Constitutional court
concepts.summary: A court whose job is to review laws against the constitution, as in Austria and Germany.

concepts.title: Judicial independence
concepts.summary: Tenure during good behaviour and pay that cannot be reduced, so that judges can resist the other branches.

concepts.title: Review not appeal
concepts.summary: In review of an official decision the court asks whether it was lawful; it does not usually retake the decision.

concepts.title: Plurality (first past the post)
concepts.summary: In each single-member district the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority.

concepts.title: D'Hondt method
concepts.summary: A highest-averages method: each party's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3 and so on, and the highest quotients, as many as there are seats, win.

concepts.title: Largest remainder method
concepts.summary: Each party's votes are divided by a quota; each party gets the whole number, and leftover seats go to the largest fractional remainders. With the Hare quota (votes divided by seats) it is Hamilton's method.

concepts.title: Droop quota
concepts.summary: Total votes divided by the number of seats plus one; more than that guarantees a seat. As a share it is 1 over k plus 1.

concepts.title: Gallagher index
concepts.summary: The square root of half the sum of the squared differences between each party's vote percent and seat percent.

concepts.title: Faction (Madison)
concepts.summary: A number of citizens, a majority or a minority, united by a common passion or interest against others' rights or the community's interests.

concepts.title: Republic (Madison)
concepts.summary: A government in which a small number of elected citizens act for the rest, which can cover a larger area than a pure democracy.

concepts.title: Political party
concepts.summary: An organisation that coordinates candidates to compete in elections and take part in governing.

concepts.title: Interest or advocacy group
concepts.summary: An organisation that seeks to influence public opinion and policy without, as a rule, running candidates.

concepts.title: Free rider problem
concepts.summary: People gain from a group's success without joining or paying, which weakens the group.

concepts.title: Agenda setting
concepts.summary: The stage at which problems that need government attention are identified and ranked.

concepts.title: Policy cycle
concepts.summary: A sequence of stages: agenda setting, policy formulation, legitimation, implementation and evaluation.

concepts.title: Legitimation
concepts.summary: The gathering of approval for a policy from an executive, a legislature or the public, through consultation or referendum.

concepts.title: Government budget
concepts.summary: A projection of revenue and spending for a period; it does not itself appropriate funds.

concepts.title: Deficit
concepts.summary: Spending above receipts, usually financed by borrowing, which builds up as debt.

concepts.title: Bureaucracy
concepts.summary: The system in which civil servants, not elected officials, put laws and regulations into effect.

concepts.title: Mill's principle
concepts.summary: Power may rightfully be used against a member of a community, against his will, only to prevent harm to others; his own good is not enough.

concepts.title: Tyranny of the majority
concepts.summary: Oppression of a minority or of individuals by a ruling majority; Mill and Tocqueville use the phrase and differ in emphasis.

concepts.title: Social tyranny
concepts.summary: Pressure by prevailing opinion and feeling, without legal penalties, that Mill says can be more formidable than political oppression.

concepts.title: Civil liberties
concepts.summary: Fundamental rights and freedoms that governments pledge not to restrict without due process of law.

concepts.title: State of emergency
concepts.summary: A power in many constitutions to suspend some rights in exceptional circumstances, which the pack says has been abused.

concepts.title: Federal state
concepts.summary: A state that divides governing powers between a central government and regional governments, in a constitution.

concepts.title: Unitary state
concepts.summary: A state in which the central government is the supreme authority; regions exercise only powers it chooses to delegate.

concepts.title: Devolution
concepts.summary: Delegation of powers by a central government to regions, which the central government can alter.

concepts.title: Residual powers
concepts.summary: The powers not listed in the constitution; they go to the states in Germany and the United States, to the centre in Canada and India.

concepts.title: Double majority
concepts.summary: A rule that an amendment needs a majority of voters nationally and a majority in a majority of the states.

concepts.title: Sovereignty
concepts.summary: In E-IR's words, a state's claim to the exclusive right to govern its territory and to act toward other states as it sees fit.

concepts.title: International anarchy
concepts.summary: A system in which power is decentralised and no shared institutions have the right to enforce common rules; not chaos.

concepts.title: Intergovernmental organisation
concepts.summary: An organisation of states whose power rests with the member governments, not with the organisation.

concepts.title: Veto
concepts.summary: A negative vote by one of the five permanent members, which blocks a draft resolution however many other votes it has.

concepts.title: Realism and liberalism
concepts.summary: Two theories: realists see an anarchic system in which states rely on themselves; liberals see room for cooperation and a democratic peace.

lessons.title: Why obey a state?

lead.text: Weber's definition describes a **state**, and it helps to separate that word from two others that often stand in for it. A state is a political unit that holds sovereignty over its own territory, which makes it closer to a legal abstraction than to any group of people you could point to. A **nation** is something else: it is a matter of political identity and of cultural or historical ties, and it has no borders, officials or claim to a monopoly of force of the kind a state makes.

The third word is **government**. Governments are organisations of people, and their relationship to the state is one of agency: they act for it, with its authority. The 1933 Montevideo Convention reflects this by listing a government as one of the four things a state needs, along with a permanent population, a defined territory and the capacity to enter relations with other states.

reveal.text: Governments come and go while states stay, which is why the next question is what makes people accept a state's claim to use force at all.

lead.text: What happens when nobody holds the [[monopoly|Weber's mark of a state: only its government may legitimately use force in its territory. Met in "State, nation and government".]]? Suppose armed groups control most of a country's provinces, each running its own courts and setting up tax posts on the roads, while the government in the capital can only watch. On Weber's definition that government has lost the monopoly of the legitimate use of force, and one definition of a **failed state**, Samuels's, says much the same: sovereignty over the territory it claims has collapsed, or never worked in the first place.

The political theorist Ross Mittiga draws a conclusion about legitimacy from cases like this. He proposes two parts. **Foundational legitimacy** is a government's capacity to guarantee its citizens' safety and security, and **contingent legitimacy** is what a government has when it exercises power in acceptable ways. A government that cannot perform the basic security functions, Mittiga says, fails the test of legitimacy and may not even count as a government, so the security question comes first.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows two invented governments through the two questions in order. One fails on security, so the second question is never reached, and the other passes on security and then meets a different test, which is how it uses its power.

diagram.alt: Two stacked questions about a government, security first and then acceptable use of power. In the first view a government that cannot keep its citizens safe fails the first question and the second is never reached. In the second a government passes the first and fails the second.

lead.text: Thomas Hobbes gave the security answer in its sharpest form in *Leviathan*, which he wrote during the English Civil War and published in 1651. Agreements between people, he said, are of little use alone, because an agreement with no sword behind it amounts to words only and cannot make anyone safe. A promise to keep the peace holds only when some power stands ready to punish a breach.

He then closes off an easy reply. Suppose a great multitude of people could simply agree to observe justice and the other laws of nature without any power above them to hold them all in check. Then, Hobbes says, there would be no need of a civil government or commonwealth at all, since there would be peace without subjection. A commonwealth exists because that supposition fails, and he defines it as one person whose acts a great multitude have authorised, each agreeing with the rest, so that he can use their strength and means for their peace and common defence.

John Locke published the *Second Treatise of Government* anonymously in 1689, and he starts from consent. Men being by nature free, equal and independent, he says, nobody can be put under the political power of another without their own **consent**. The only route out of natural liberty and into civil society is to agree with others to join together in a community, so as to live comfortably, safely and peaceably and to enjoy their property securely.

Locke still wants a government with strength behind it. Among the things he says are missing without one is the power to back a just sentence and see it carried out, because those who have done an injustice will, wherever they can, make it good by force, and that makes punishment dangerous to those who attempt it. Wikipedia's article on legitimacy reads Locke as relying on both explicit and implicit consent of the governed.

reveal.text: Locke reasons from what the people lent and what it was lent for, and the next screen sets out his test and says who applies it.

lead.text: Locke's picture is one of trust. The people deputise a government to secure their property and keep them from arbitrary power, and it holds its power as a trustee. When legislators set out to destroy the people's property, or to make them slaves of arbitrary power, he writes, they place themselves at war with the people, who are released from owing them any more obedience.

The same test reaches a quieter kind of breach. If a ruler alters the electors or the ways of election without the people's consent and against their common interest, then those chosen are not the legislature the people appointed, and to regulate the candidates and electors and remodel the ways of election, Locke asks, is to cut the government off at its roots. He also says who decides whether a trust has been broken. The people shall be judge, since whoever deputes a trustee must keep the power to discard him when he fails.
One objection to all this comes from David Hume. He contested the idea that legitimacy rests on consent, arguing that nobody ever gave that consent and nobody could take it back by leaving.

reveal.text: The two answers are about what a state must be able to do, and Weber's types, on the next screen, are about why the people it rules accept that it may.

lead.text: Hobbes and Locke tell us what a state has to supply, and Mittiga's two parts give a way to line up their answers, with Hobbes's security as the foundational part and Locke's concern that power be used for the ends it was lent for as the contingent part. Weber asked a different question, which is why the people a state rules accept its right to rule. For him a state is legitimate when its subjects think its claim to power and authority is valid, and he named three bases for that belief.

**Traditional legitimacy** rests on custom and habit. The rule is accepted as part of history, and it continues since it is simply how society has always done things. **Charismatic legitimacy** rests on the ideas and personal qualities of a leader, and since the authority comes from the person, a charismatic government usually has weak institutions and usually disappears when the leader is no longer in power. **Rational-legal legitimacy** rests on institutional procedure, with institutions that make and enforce law in the public interest, and it holds as long as the public trusts the government to abide by the law.

afterFigure.text: None of the three requires that the ruled have voted. Weber held that democracy was unnecessary for establishing legitimacy, which can rest on codified laws, customs and cultural principles instead of popular suffrage.

diagram.alt: A table with three columns, traditional, charismatic and rational-legal legitimacy. One row says what obedience rests on in each: custom and habit, a leader's personal qualities, institutional procedure and law. A second row says what follows: continuity, weak institutions that usually disappear with the leader, and public trust that the government will abide by the law.

reveal.text: Which basis a regime claims tells you what would weaken it: a lapse of custom, the loss of a leader, or a loss of faith in the procedures.

lead.text: Weber's types describe the beliefs of the ruled, and real states add detail. The article on legitimacy stresses that establishing legitimacy is not simply transactional: services, elections and the rule of law do not automatically grant it, because it depends on what citizens perceive and expect of the state, and what legitimises a state differs from one country to the next. In one study, by McCullough and colleagues, the service most closely tied to the state's legitimacy was public water in Nepal and health care in Pakistan. States are not the only builders of legitimacy either, and armed groups in a conflict zone may build it more successfully than the state among some parts of the population.

It follows that popularity is a poor guide to survival. Unpopular regimes can survive, the article says, because a small, influential elite considers them legitimate. The Mandate of Heaven in Chinese political philosophy is a basis of this non-democratic kind: from the time of the Zhou dynasty, a ruler's right to govern was taken to come from it, and an unjust ruler who lost it lost that right. The political scientist Robert Dahl pictured legitimacy as a reservoir, in which stability holds while the water stays at a given level and legitimacy is endangered when it falls below the level required.

reveal.text: Popularity and legitimacy are different things, which is why the same question can be asked of a regime that holds elections and of one that holds none.

lessons.orientation: Say what a state's claim to obedience rests on, apply Locke's test of broken trust to a described government, and use Weber's three types of legitimacy to explain why obedience holds or fails.
lessons.nextAction: Classify a described regime by who rules and whose good the rule serves, and by the four categories that political scientists use today.

blocks.text: The most commonly used definition of a state, Max Weber's, says that it is a compulsory political organisation whose government keeps the monopoly of the legitimate use of force in its territory. Two words in that definition carry most of the weight. *Monopoly* says that nobody else in the territory may use force without the state's permission, and *legitimate* says that people accept the state's claim to do so, which makes legitimacy a fact about what people believe as well as a fact about what the state can enforce.

That raises a question you can ask of any government you read about: what makes people accept its claim, and what happens when they stop? Hobbes, Locke and Weber answer it differently, and the differences show up when you look at a real government and ask what its right to rule rests on and whether that basis is holding.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a described state's claim to obedience rests on, and to judge whether that claim still holds.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you tell a government that is merely strong from one that people accept, and to see what would make each of them fail.

recap.keyIdea: A state's claim to obedience can rest on security, on consent and the acceptable use of power, or on custom, a leader or lawful procedure, and each basis fails in its own way.

blocks.text: Weber's definition makes legitimacy part of what a state is: a monopoly of force that the people it rules accept as the state's to use. Hobbes explains why a society needs that monopoly, and Locke adds that the power is held in trust, so a government that attacks the property and liberty it was set up to protect, or that alters the elections that appoint it, can lose the right to be obeyed.

Weber's three types ask what sort of belief supports the rule, whether in custom, in a leader or in procedure. A regime can survive without popularity when a small, influential elite regards it as legitimate, and any regime can lose legitimacy when it stops providing what its citizens expect of it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks a related question about whole governments: who rules, whose good the rule serves, and how political scientists sort the regimes of the world today.

lessons.title: Classifying a regime

lead.text: Aristotle began by noting that any government must place supreme authority over the entire state somewhere, and that it can rest with one person, with a few, or with many. His first question about any constitution is therefore *how many* hold the supreme power, and his second is *whose good* they have in view. When the one, the few or the many use that authority for the common good, he says, the state is well governed, and when they look only to their own interest the form is a wrong one.

Three answers to the first question and two to the second make six forms, and the names here are Jowett's, from his translation of 1885. Rule by one person for the common good is a **kingdom**, rule by a few is an **aristocracy**, and when the citizens at large rule with the public good in view the translation calls it simply **a state**. Each good form has a corrupt twin, which is **tyranny** for the kingdom, **oligarchy** for the aristocracy and **democracy** for the state, and Aristotle says what each corrupt form looks to: a tyranny to the good of one man, an oligarchy to the rich alone, and a democracy to the poor alone.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the six names in a grid, and its bottom right corner is the one to notice: democracy is the *corrupt* form of rule by the many, so Aristotle's word does not mean what it means in the news today.

diagram.alt: A grid of Aristotle's six forms of government. Rows are rule by one, a few or the many. In the column where rulers look to the common good the forms are kingdom, aristocracy and a state. In the column where rulers look only to their own interest they are tyranny, oligarchy and democracy.
diagram.caption: Aristotle's six forms as Jowett names them. Democracy, bottom right, is the corrupt form of rule by the many.

lead.text: The names oligarchy and democracy sound like a count, with few rulers in one and many in the other, but Aristotle refines them so that the count drops out. If the rich hold the government, whether they are few or many, he says, it is an oligarchy, and if the poor hold it, it is a democracy. What separates the two corrupt forms is *who* rules, the rich or the poor.

His test for a right form does not depend on numbers either. Governments that keep the common good in sight are soundly founded and just, he says, while those that look only to the good of the rulers rest on wrong principles, so a government of any size can be judged by the same question.

reveal.text: Aristotle's democracy is a corrupt form, so the modern use of the word needs its own definitions, and the next screen gives two.

lead.text: Today the word has a different meaning from Aristotle's: it names a government whose political power belongs to the people of a state. A **narrow** definition asks only that rulers be chosen in competitive elections, and **broader** definitions add guarantees of civil liberties and human rights. Which definition you use decides which countries you count.

The broader idea is what people mean by **liberal democracy**. In its common form the majority exercises power through representatives, while a constitution and a supreme court hold the majority in check and shield the minority, typically by securing individual rights such as freedom of speech and association. An **illiberal democracy**, also called a procedural democracy, holds the elections but lacks things like the rule of law, safeguards for minorities, independent courts and a genuine separation of powers.

The opposite pole is **authoritarian** government, and the minimal definition of it is the lack of free and competitive elections to the legislature, to the executive, or to both. Authoritarian states often keep institutions that look democratic, such as parties, legislatures and elections, and these may be managed to entrench the rulers, with fraudulent or non-competitive elections.

So a report that a country holds elections tells you less than it seems to. One way to keep that in view is to treat democracy and authoritarianism as poles at the two ends of a scale, which leaves room for a democracy with some authoritarian elements and for an authoritarian system with some democratic ones.

reveal.text: The regime data turn that question into definitions, and the next screen reads them as three questions asked one after another.

lead.text: The regime chart on Our World in Data, which draws on the V-Dem Regimes of the World classification, sorts country-years into four categories. Its definitions can be read as three questions asked in turn. That is one way of reading their wording, since the chart page does not describe the procedure the coders follow. The first asks whether citizens are entitled to choose both the chief executive and the legislature in multi-party elections. If they do not, the regime is a **closed autocracy**.

If they do, the second question is whether the elections are meaningful, free and fair, which depends on freedoms such as association and expression. If those freedoms are lacking the regime is an **electoral autocracy**, and if they are present it is an **electoral democracy**. The third question asks whether citizens also have individual and minority rights and equality before the law, and whether the legislature and the courts constrain the executive. A regime where all of that holds is a **liberal democracy**.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows each category through the questions in turn. A regime stops at the first question it fails, so an electoral democracy is one that passes the first two and fails the third.

diagram.alt: A chain of three questions with four outcomes. If citizens cannot choose the chief executive and legislature in multi-party elections, the regime is a closed autocracy. If they can but the elections are not meaningful, free and fair, it is an electoral autocracy. If rights and limits on the executive are missing, it is an electoral democracy. If those exist too, it is a liberal democracy.
diagram.caption: The three questions in order, with the route for each category highlighted. Use the buttons to follow each route.

reveal.text: Real regimes are not always as tidy as these six descriptions, and the last screen is about what to say when one falls between the boxes.

lead.text: Some regimes mix the two poles. A **hybrid regime** is a political system with a combination of autocratic and democratic features, often the result of an incomplete transition from one kind of regime to the other, and it can hold regular elections while keeping political repression. Pippa Norris describes one as a system with weak checks on the executive, flawed or suspended elections, a fragmented opposition, state restrictions on the media and civil society, curbs on the judiciary and disregard for the rule of law.

**Competitive authoritarianism** is one kind of hybrid regime. Elections are held regularly and the opposition can operate openly without much risk of being exiled or jailed, yet the regime falls short on free elections, solid civil liberties and an even contest. Parties do not settle the matter either, since they matter in autocracies as well as in democracies, and in autocracies a single governing party is common. A description that fits no box neatly is still informative, because it says which defining features are present and which are missing.

reveal.text: A description that names its features lets you say how far a regime sits from each pole, whether or not it has a box.

lessons.orientation: Classify a described regime by who rules and whose good the rule serves, and by the four categories of the regime data, and say why a description that fits between boxes is still informative.
lessons.nextAction: Read a regime series, a population count and a turnout series with their definitions in hand, and say what a number can and cannot show.

blocks.text: A news report says that a country holds elections, and so it is a democracy. Is that a good argument? Elections are held in regimes of very different kinds, including authoritarian ones whose elections are managed to keep their rulers in place, so the report leaves out a good deal of what you would need to know.

Aristotle, writing in the fourth century BC, started from two questions about who holds the supreme power and whose good it serves, and modern regime data start from what citizens are free to choose and what limits the rulers. Together they give you a way to describe a regime from a few facts and to say precisely where a description is uncertain.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a described regime by who rules and whose good it serves, and by the four categories used in regime data.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you say what is missing from a claim like 'it holds elections, so it is a democracy'.

recap.keyIdea: A regime can be classified by who rules and whose good the rule serves, and by what citizens can choose and what limits their rulers.

blocks.text: Aristotle asked how many hold the supreme power and whose good they serve, and his democracy is the corrupt rule of the poor for themselves, kept apart from oligarchy by wealth, whatever the number of rulers. The modern categories ask whether citizens can choose their rulers in multi-party elections, whether those elections are meaningful, free and fair, and whether rights and constraints on the executive exist.
Regimes that mix democratic and autocratic features are hybrids, and a description that fits no single box still reports which features are present and which are missing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the data behind those categories: how to read a series that experts have coded, what a count and a share each say, and what a number cannot show.

lessons.title: Reading regime and turnout data

lead.text: The regime data in this lesson come from the Varieties of Democracy project, V-Dem, which draws on assessments by around 3,500 country experts of political institutions and of how well rights are protected. Our World in Data charts the result as the four categories you met in the last lesson. A **coded series** is built by assigning a category to every country and every year against written definitions, so that when a country's category changes, what has happened is that the coders judged a defining feature, such as freedom of association, to have appeared or gone. A change is the coders' judgement against the definitions, and it carries no official verdict on a government.
Read down one country's rows and you find **runs**, stretches of years that share a category. The figure draws the runs for seven countries from 1900 to 2025.

afterFigure.text: Brazil and Egypt change category several times, and the runs differ in length as much as in colour. Germany's bar has a dashed stretch in the middle, which the next screens take up.

reveal.text: The order comes from the first run of liberal democracy in each bar, whatever category the country was in before.

lead.text: Look at Germany's bar. It shows closed autocracy until 1944 and picks up again in 1991, because the file has no rows for Germany from 1945 to 1990. A **gap** like this tells you only that the file holds no category for those years. It cannot tell you that Germany had no regime in them, or that Germany stayed what it was in 1944, and the file gives no reason.

Changes need the same care. A series can switch back and forth, as Egypt's does between electoral autocracy and closed autocracy, and each switch is the coders' judgement that a defining feature changed. Where the file shows a recent change in some country, it says that the category changed and does not say why, so a reader who supplies a cause is adding something the data do not contain.

reveal.text: Gaps are the simplest case of a number that cannot be taken at face value, and the next screens turn from categories to counts of people.

lead.text: The regime data also come as counts of people. For every year the file gives the number of the world's people living under each of the four categories, plus a very small group with no data, and the five groups added together make the total the file covers. A **count** says how many people, and a **share** divides a count by a total, so the two answer different questions and can move in opposite directions.

Closed autocracies show it. About 2.02 billion people lived in them in 1990 and about 2.22 billion in 2022, so the count rose. The world's population grew faster, from about 5.32 billion to about 8.01 billion, so the share fell from 38.1 percent to 27.7 percent. The figure draws the two years twice. In the first view each bar is as wide as the population the file covers in that year, which is how you compare counts, and in the second both bars are stretched to the same width, which is how you compare shares.

afterFigure.text: A claim that closed autocracy grew and a claim that it shrank can therefore both be true of the same two years, because they are claims about different numbers.

In the second both bars are the same width, and the closed autocracy segment is a smaller part of the 2022 bar than of the 1990 bar.

steps.headline: What share of the world's people lived in an electoral or a liberal democracy in 1990?

workedSteps.text: Add the two counts that make up the democracies. For 1990 the file gives 1,416,883,613 people in electoral democracies and 812,949,463 in liberal democracies.
A share needs a total to divide by, and the choice of total changes the answer, so decide what goes underneath.
The file covers 5,316,486,263 people in 1990, with all five groups added together, so the working divides the democracies' count by that total.

About 41.9 percent of the world's people lived in an electoral or a liberal democracy in 1990. The same steps give 29.3 percent for 2022, and the series peaks in 2001 at 53.5 percent. Wikipedia's claim that less than half the world lived in a democracy in 2022 is true on these counts, and the counts say how much less: a little under three in ten.

reveal.text: A share is only as meaningful as what it is a share of, which matters even more for turnout, where the total is a list of registered voters.

lead.text: Voter turnout is another share, and its definition fixes what it can tell you. The series takes turnout to be the proportion of registered voters who voted in a national election, using the official results. The **denominator**, the thing a percentage is a percentage of, is therefore the register, so a figure says how many of the people on the register voted and says nothing on its own about how many adults there are.

Australia's turnout in 2022 was 89.74 percent and Sweden's was 84.21 percent, and both are coded as liberal democracies in that year. Turnout is easy to read as a measure of democracy, but a high figure only means that a large share of the people on the register voted. The series carries no information about whether the election was free.

reveal.text: Turnout and category answer different questions, and the next screen is about the checks that tell you whether a single number can be used at all.

lead.text: A series can contain a value that needs checking before you use it. Suppose a table gave one country's turnout as exactly 61.4 percent in five elections in a row. Five identical results from five different elections are unlikely, so the sensible response is to check the source before drawing any conclusion. The repeats are neither a finding that turnout stood still nor a reason to discard the whole country. We call a value, or a run of identical values, that is unlikely enough to need this treatment an **anomaly**.

Definitions need the same checking. Indices of democracy often disagree, and occasionally they reach contradictory conclusions about the same event. Part of the reason is that measurement follows the underlying idea of democracy: minimalist approaches look at free and fair elections, while maximalist ones add further values, among them human rights, deliberation, economic results and the capacity of the state. Indices that use different definitions and methods also often disagree about which countries are hybrid regimes, so two figures for one country may not conflict, because they are about different things.

reveal.text: Checking a value before using it is the first step, and the last screen is about what a correct number still cannot show.

lead.text: A third series measures the percentage of women among the members of the lower chamber, or the only chamber, of the national legislature. It is not about regimes, which makes it a clean test of what a number can carry. In 2025 it gives 45 percent for Sweden and 27 percent for the world as a whole.

Wikipedia's article on [[proportional representation|Electoral systems in which parties win seats in proportion to the votes they receive. The course takes them up in "From votes to seats".]] reports a gain of about 8 percent, on average, in the women elected under it compared with other systems. An average over many countries describes the pattern across the set, and single countries can sit on either side of it. Two countries cannot show a cause either, because testing the claim would need many countries, the electoral system of each, and a way to set aside everything else that differs between them.

reveal.text: A number can be accurate and still be asked to carry more than it can, and checking for that is the habit of reading data with its definition in hand.

lessons.orientation: Read a regime series, a population count and a turnout series with their definitions in hand, and say what a number can and cannot show.
lessons.nextAction: Use Montesquieu's definitions to say which power an act belongs to, and use his and Madison's arguments to test a described arrangement.

blocks.text: Wikipedia says that less than half of the world's population lived in a democracy in 2022, and it cites two democracy indices for the claim. The regime data on Our World in Data, built on V-Dem's four categories, put the figure at just under three in ten. The two statements are consistent, but only the second is a number you can check. Where does such a number come from, and what does it leave out?

Every number about regimes carries a definition, and someone's decision about which country belongs in which category. Before you use a figure from a table, find out what was counted, who decided, what a percentage is a percentage of, and what the table does not say.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a regime series, a population count and a turnout figure with their definitions in hand, and say what a number can and cannot show.
intro.whyItMatters: Figures about governments look exact, and knowing what each one measures stops you from drawing a conclusion it cannot support.

recap.keyIdea: A number about regimes is only as good as its definition, so read what it counts, what it is a share of, and what it leaves out.

blocks.text: A coded series records experts' judgements against written definitions, a gap in it says only that the file has no data, and a count can rise while a share falls because the total grew faster. Turnout is a share of registered voters, so it says how many of the people on the register voted and nothing about whether the vote was free.

A value that looks too regular is a reason to check the source, and indices that define democracy differently can disagree without either being wrong. An average over many countries cannot be tested, or explained, by two countries alone.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the constitutions behind these categories, starting with Montesquieu's argument that liberty depends on keeping three powers apart.

lessons.title: Montesquieu and the separation of powers

lead.text: Montesquieu begins from a claim about every government: it has three sorts of power. The **legislative power** is the power by which a prince or magistrate enacts laws, whether temporary or lasting, and amends or repeals those already made. The **executive power** is the power to make peace or war, to exchange embassies with other states, to keep the public safe and to guard against invasion. The third, by which he punishes crimes and settles the disputes that arise between individuals, Montesquieu calls the **judiciary power**.

His executive power is wider than the word usually suggests. It covers foreign affairs and defence as well as carrying out the laws, so the question of who holds the executive power of a country includes who decides on peace or war.

diagram.alt: Three columns for Montesquieu's three powers. The legislative power makes, amends and repeals laws. The executive power covers peace and war, embassies, public safety and defence against invasion. The judiciary power punishes crimes and settles disputes between individuals.

reveal.text: Sorting acts is the easy half of Montesquieu's idea, and the harder half is what follows when one body does the work of more than one.

lead.text: Montesquieu's argument starts with the judges. There is no liberty, he says, if the judiciary power is not separated from the legislative and the executive. Joined to the legislative power it would leave the life and liberty of the subject exposed to arbitrary control, because the judge would then be the legislator, and joined to the executive the judge could act with violence and oppression.

He generalises the point: everything would be lost, he writes, if one man or one body, whether of nobles or of the people, held all three powers. He contrasts the kingdoms of his own time. Most of those in Europe, he says, have a moderate government since the prince holds the first two powers and leaves the third to his subjects, while in Turkey, where all three rest with the Sultan himself, the people endure the worst oppression. We call the principle behind the contrast **separation of powers**, the idea that the three powers should be held by different persons or bodies.

reveal.text: Montesquieu's remedy is to keep the powers apart, and Madison asked what would make them stay apart in practice.

lead.text: Madison takes up the question in *The Federalist* No. 51, published in 1788. Lines drawn on paper are not enough, he argues. The best protection against a slow gathering of the powers in one department is to give those who run each department the constitutional means and the personal motives to resist the encroachments of the others, so that ambition is made to counteract ambition. His reason is that people who were angels would need no government, and angels governing people would need no controls on it. Since men govern men, a government must first be able to control the governed and then be obliged to control itself.

The means can be shared powers. Montesquieu himself says the executive should have a share in lawmaking through the power of rejecting, and the presidential veto is a familiar example of a legislative power in the hands of the executive. A separation of powers tempered by these **checks and balances** lets the branches overlap, where a rigid reading would let no branch use another's power and no person sit in more than one branch.

Separation also needs separate sources of authority. Wikipedia's article, reading Montesquieu, says that if the legislature appoints the executive and the judges there is no separation, because whoever can appoint can also remove.

diagram.alt: Three views of the three powers. In the first each is held by a separate body. In the second an arrow runs from the executive to the legislature, marked veto, showing the executive rejecting bills. In the third arrows run from the legislature to the executive and the judiciary, marked appoints, showing a legislature that appoints the others and can therefore remove them.

reveal.text: Checks are one answer to the question of how to keep the powers apart, and some writers rejected the question.

lead.text: Not everyone thought separation wise. The British constitutional expert Walter Bagehot held that the English Constitution's efficient secret was how closely its executive and legislative powers are joined, to the point of **fusion**, and that its merit lay in what he called their singular approximation, whatever the textbooks said about separating them. Thomas Paine denied that English liberty was secured by checks and balances, saying that England's freedom from oppression came from the make-up of its people rather than from the form of its government, and Wikipedia's article records that Hobbes also strongly opposed separation of powers.

Checks have a cost as well: where the veto players in different branches are not aligned, vetoes can produce gridlock. Even so, the separation of the judiciary from the other two is the norm in modern democracies, while many countries keep the legislative and executive branches joined, following the principle of **fusion of powers** instead.

reveal.text: The two writers agree on what the arrangement is, and the last screen asks you to apply both of their views to one invented country.
Whether such an arrangement endangers liberty depends on which of the writers you follow, and either can be applied to a country described in these terms.

lessons.orientation: Use Montesquieu's definitions to say which power an act belongs to, use his and Madison's arguments to test a described arrangement, and set Bagehot's opposite view beside them.
lessons.reviewLabel: Montesquieu and the separation of powers
lessons.nextAction: Say which body holds a named power, whether another body must agree, and what checks it, from the text of two constitutions.

blocks.text: In *The Spirit of Laws*, published in 1748, Montesquieu wrote that everything would be lost if a single man or body, noble or popular, made the laws, carried out public resolutions and tried the cases of individuals. It is a large claim, and it brings a puzzle with it: if the danger is that one hand holds all three jobs, must they be kept entirely apart, or may one body share in the work of another?

Madison took up the question in *The Federalist* in 1788, and other writers disagreed with both of them, Walter Bagehot among them, who found the merit of the British system in the opposite arrangement. Weighing these arguments is a skill, and it rests on a simpler one that comes first, which is deciding which of the three jobs a particular act belongs to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which of Montesquieu's three powers an act belongs to, and to test a described arrangement against his and Madison's arguments.
intro.whyItMatters: It gives you a way to ask of any government who can make a law, who can carry it out, and who can judge you under it.

recap.keyIdea: Montesquieu's three powers are told apart by what an act does, and his argument, with Madison's, is that liberty depends on how the powers are divided and how each is able to resist the rest.

blocks.text: The legislative power makes and repeals laws, the executive makes peace or war and provides for security, and the judiciary punishes crimes and settles disputes between individuals. Montesquieu held that the judiciary must stand apart from both of the others, and that one hand holding all three ends liberty.

Madison added that separation needs means and motives, which shared powers such as the veto supply, and that a legislature that appoints the others holds the power to revoke. Bagehot, Paine and Hobbes show that the idea has critics, and the cost of checks is gridlock when the branches are not aligned.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson applies these questions to two real texts, the United States Constitution of 1787 and the Australian Constitution of 1900, and asks which body holds each power in them.

lessons.title: Reading a constitution

lead.text: Both texts begin by saying where legislative power rests, and both use the same verb, **vested**. Article 1 of the United States Constitution says that all the legislative powers it grants are vested in a Congress, which consists of a Senate and a House of Representatives. The Australian text says that the legislative power of the Commonwealth is vested in a Federal Parliament made up of the Queen together with a Senate and a House of Representatives. The two differ in a way that matters, since in Australia the monarch, whom the 1900 text calls the Queen, is part of the body that legislates.

These are the texts as they were first written, the United States Constitution of 1787 before any amendment and the Australian Constitution Act as enacted in 1900. They show how each document first placed the powers, and they say nothing about what changed afterwards. Both go on to vest the executive power and the judicial power in the same way, and reading a power means finding the clause that vests it and then the clauses that qualify it.

afterFigure.text: In each text the power is vested in the body as a whole, and the figure shows who counts as part of it.

diagram.alt: Two views of where legislative power sits. In the United States text it is vested in Congress, which consists of the Senate and the House of Representatives. In the Australian text it is vested in the Federal Parliament, which has a Senate, a House of Representatives and the Queen as its parts.

reveal.text: A clause can place a power in one person and let another use it, and the Australian text goes on to say who that other person works through.

lead.text: The Australian text lets the Governor-General appoint officers to administer the departments of state. These officers hold office during the Governor-General's pleasure, they are members of the Federal Executive Council, and they are the Queen's Ministers of State. A further clause makes membership of the Senate or the House of Representatives a condition of keeping a ministry beyond three months, once the first general election has passed. The text also leaves the Governor-General a discretion over whether to assent to a bill.

You will not find the office of Prime Minister in it, because the words Prime Minister and Cabinet do not appear anywhere in the 1900 text. Wikipedia's article on parliamentary systems describes the practice of the Westminster systems: prime ministers are usually the leader of the largest party in parliament, and formally the head of state, whether monarch, governor-general or president, holds the prerogative of appointing them. What a constitution's words provide and how a government is actually run are two things, and the gap between **text and practice** is what a careful reader looks for.

reveal.text: Reading the text is where an argument about a constitution begins, and powers that need two bodies to agree are where it usually turns.

lead.text: Many powers need more than one body to agree. A bill becomes law in the United States only if both houses pass it and it is then presented to the President. If he approves he signs it, and if not he returns it with his objections to the house where it began, which enters them in its journal and reconsiders it. If two thirds of that house then agree, the bill goes with the objections to the other house, and if two thirds of that house approve it too, it becomes law. This is the veto of the last lesson, the executive's share in lawmaking by rejecting, together with the legislature's power to overcome it.

Two more powers are shared. The President can make treaties with the Senate's advice and consent, if two thirds of the Senators who are present agree, and he can nominate and, with the same advice and consent, appoint ambassadors, other public ministers, consuls and Supreme Court judges, along with other officers. **Advice and consent** is the Senate's share. Money bills carry a limit of their own, and in the United States bills for raising revenue must begin in the House of Representatives, though the Senate may propose or concur in amendments, while the Australian text says that proposed laws appropriating revenue or imposing taxation may not originate in the Senate.

lead.text: Most other powers in the American text can be read one at a time. Congress has the power to lay and collect taxes and duties, to declare war and to raise and support armies, though money for the armies may not be voted for longer than two years at a time. The President commands the army and navy as commander in chief, and he can grant reprieves and pardons for federal offences, though not in cases of impeachment. The judicial power extends to all cases arising under the Constitution, federal laws and treaties.

Removal is divided in the same way. The House of Representatives has the sole power of **impeachment**, which is the accusation, and the Senate has the sole power to try all impeachments, with the Chief Justice presiding when the President is tried. A conviction needs the agreement of two thirds of those members present, and the President, the Vice President and all civil officers lose their offices if they are impeached and convicted of treason, bribery or other high crimes.

reveal.text: Knowing who holds a power and who must agree leaves the question of what restrains it, and both texts have a rule about money.

lead.text: A rule about money reaches every other power, because armies, courts and offices all have to be paid for. The United States text says that money may leave the Treasury only through **appropriations** that a law has made, and that a regular statement and account of receipts and expenditures of all public money is to be published from time to time. An appropriation is a law that authorises money to be drawn, so the executive cannot spend what the legislature has not authorised.

The Australian text deals with money in a clause of its own, and it also gives a check on the courts: its judges can be removed only if both Houses of Parliament, in the same session, petition the Governor-General in Council to do so for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. In both texts the removal of a high officer needs the agreement of more than one body, which is how a text builds a check into the power to remove.

reveal.text: A rule about money is one place where a text builds in a check, and a clause about who may sit where is another.
The two clauses give the two sides of the last lesson's argument in the words of two real constitutions.

lessons.orientation: From the text of the United States Constitution (1787) and the Australian Constitution (1900 as enacted), say which body holds a named power, whether another body must agree, and what checks it.
lessons.nextAction: Classify a country's system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed.

blocks.text: Open the United States Constitution of 1787 at Article 1 and the first sentence says where legislative power rests, which is in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. Open the Australian Constitution Act of 1900 and its opening clauses do the same for a Federal Parliament, and make the Queen part of that Parliament. Both documents use the same verb, and a reader who follows it through the text can say which body holds a power, who has to agree before it is used, and what checks it.

That is a different skill from knowing how a country is run. A constitution is written text, and the way a system works in practice can use offices that the words never mention, so reading one well means asking what the text says and what it leaves unsaid.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say, from the text of two constitutions, which body holds a named power, whether another body must agree, and what checks it.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you check a claim about who can do what against the words of the document itself.

recap.keyIdea: A constitution says where each power is vested, which bodies must agree before it is used and what checks it, and its words can differ from the practice of a government.

blocks.text: In both texts a power is vested in a named body, and the clauses that follow say who must agree and what limits it: the Senate's advice and consent for treaties and appointments, two thirds of each house to override a veto, and a law of appropriation before any money leaves the treasury. Impeachment in the United States and an address from both Houses in Australia give the power to remove officers to more than one body.

The Australian text vests executive power in the Queen, exercised through the Governor-General, and never uses the words Prime Minister or Cabinet, so a text and the practice around it are two separate things to learn.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson classifies systems by how the head of government is chosen and removed, which turns the contrast between these two texts into three named types.

lessons.title: Parliamentary, presidential and mixed systems

steps.headline: Two questions about the head of government

lead.text: Every country has someone who leads the executive branch from day to day, and we'll call that person the **head of government**. It might be a prime minister, a president or an officeholder with some other title, and as we'll see the title says less than you'd expect. What does tell you something is the answer to two questions: how does this person come to office, and who has the power to remove them?

The answers fall into three patterns, and each is a different reply to the question Montesquieu raised about how closely the executive and the legislature should be tied. In one pattern the head of government depends on the legislature. In another they stand apart from it, and in a third a president and a prime minister share the executive and only one of them answers to the legislature. We'll take the patterns in that order.

Start with the pattern that has the plainest rule. In a parliamentary system the head of government holds office only while a majority of parliament supports them, and that support is called **confidence**. If parliament passes a vote of no confidence the head of government loses it, and their time in office ends. Their authority to lead comes from being able to command that majority, so asking who chooses them has a built-in answer: whoever can count on parliament.

The choosing can still involve more than one actor. In Germany the federal president nominates a candidate for head of government and the Bundestag votes on the nomination. The president names someone, but parliament decides, so the head of government still depends on a parliamentary vote, and that dependence is what makes the system parliamentary.

The second pattern reverses the first. In a **presidential system** the head of government is elected by citizens, directly or through a group chosen for the purpose, and is not responsible to the legislature. The legislature cannot dismiss the president during their term except in extraordinary cases, so it can disagree with the president as sharply as it likes and the president still holds office until the term ends.

It's tempting to read a system off the title, and the title misleads. The article on presidential systems points out that dictators and leaders of one-party states, whether popularly elected or not, often carry the title of president. Iran adds a second warning. The article says Iran has had a modified presidential system since a constitutional reform in 1989, in which the Supreme Leader is head of state and the absolute power in the country, so a president can hold the office while the real authority sits above it. The two questions tell you how a president comes and goes. Who actually runs the country is a further question, and the constitution's own text has to answer it.

Some countries combine the two patterns. In a **semi-presidential system** a president exists alongside a prime minister and a cabinet. The president is an executive who is independent of the legislature, as in a presidential system, while the prime minister and cabinet are responsible to the legislature, as in a parliamentary one. Even when the president names the cabinet, the legislature can still force it to resign by a motion of no confidence, and that retained power is what separates this pattern from a presidential system.

The label covers two arrangements, and which one a country has depends on who can remove the prime minister. In the **premier-presidential** kind, only parliament can approve the prime minister and cabinet and only parliament can remove them, so the system sits close to a parliamentary one. In the **president-parliamentary** kind the prime minister and cabinet answer to both the president and parliament: the president can dismiss them, and parliament can remove them by a no-confidence vote, which puts the system close to a presidential one. The article lists France, Portugal and Romania under the first kind, and Russia, Taiwan and Kazakhstan under the second.

lead.text: A president and a prime minister don't always come from the same party, and when they don't the situation is called **cohabitation**, a term that began in France after it first arose in the 1980s. In 1981 France elected both a Socialist president and a Socialist legislature, but the president's term was seven years and the legislature's five. When voters chose a right-of-centre assembly in 1986, the Socialist president François Mitterrand had to work with the right-wing prime minister Jacques Chirac.

The article says cohabitation can produce an effective system of checks and balances or a period of bitter and tense stonewalling, depending on the attitudes of the two leaders, the ideologies of their parties and the demands of their supporters. It also notes that cohabitation tends to arise when the two executives are not elected at the same time or for the same term. France shortened its president's term to five years in 2000, which the article says lowers the chance of it happening.
In country K, voters elect a president every five years. The president names a prime minister and cabinet and can dismiss them, and so can parliament, by a vote of no confidence. Which family is K?
The method is to ask the two questions in turn and let the answers narrow the choice.

workedSteps.text: Ask how the head of government comes to office. K has two executives, a president elected by voters and a prime minister whom the president names, so it isn't a plain parliamentary system.
Ask who can remove the prime minister and cabinet. Parliament can, by a vote of no confidence, so the cabinet answers to the legislature.
A president with an independent executive role beside a cabinet that answers to parliament is a semi-presidential system.
The president can also dismiss the cabinet, so it answers to both. That is the president-parliamentary kind, the one that sits closer to a presidential system.

lead.text: There's a third question, about people. May the same person sit in the legislature and run a part of the executive? Montesquieu thought not: he said that if the executive power were committed to persons selected from the legislative body, there would be an end of liberty, because the same persons would hold a share in both powers.

Most Westminster systems do the opposite, in what the article calls strict monism, where ministers must be members of parliament at the same time. Australia's constitution says so in plain words: no minister of state may hold office for more than three months unless they are or become a senator or a member of the House of Representatives. The Netherlands, Slovakia and Sweden go the other way and practise **dualism**, where a member of parliament has to resign their seat on being appointed a minister, as a form of separation of powers. The United States Constitution applies the idea to every office under the United States: no person holding one may be a member of either House while in office.

That means a parliamentary system doesn't have to fuse the two branches completely. The article on the separation of powers describes Australia as semi-parliamentary, because only the House of Representatives has confidence powers, so that the Senate stands for an aspect of separation, and it says the system has been called a Washminster variation for this reason.

afterFigure.text: Each marker on the line sits where the passage about it puts it, and the line sorts arrangements without measuring them.
