lead.text: Montesquieu's remark is one side of an old argument. The British writer Walter Bagehot took the other side about the Westminster system. He called the close union, the nearly complete fusion, of the executive and legislative powers the efficient secret of the English constitution, and he said that although the books praise their separation, the merit of that constitution lay in how closely they come together.

Presidential systems have their own defenders and critics. James Wilson, who advocated for a presidential system at the constitutional convention, argued that a single chief executive gives more public accountability than a group, because it is plain who is responsible for what the executive does, and that this protects against tyranny. The article records the charge on the other side, that a presidential system can produce gridlock when the president and the legislature are in opposition, and it says this rarely happens in a parliamentary system because the prime minister is always a member of the party in power. Of semi-presidential systems it reports the criticism that they blur accountability, since there's no clear sense of who is responsible for successes and failures.

Each of these writers is arguing for something different: Montesquieu for liberty through separation, Bagehot for effective government through fusion, and Wilson for accountability through a single executive.
Apply the two questions to six invented descriptions. Each one gives you enough to place it, and a title isn't part of the evidence.

lessons.orientation: Classify a country's system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed, and say what each arrangement does to the separation Montesquieu described.
lessons.nextAction: Say what a court can do about a law or an act of the executive in a described case.

blocks.text: When the news says a government has fallen, the words can mean very different things in different countries. In some a head of government who loses the support of most of the legislature has to go, sometimes within days. In others the head of government stays until the term ends, whichever way the legislature votes. Both kinds of country have someone who runs the executive from day to day, and from outside the two look alike.

What separates them is two facts about that office: how its holder is chosen, and who has the power to remove them. Those two facts sort the world's executives into a small number of families, and they settle how much the executive and the legislature depend on each other, which is the matter Montesquieu raised in the lesson on the separation of powers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a country's system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed.
intro.whyItMatters: The same title, president or prime minister, can sit on very different offices, so a system has to be read from how the office is filled and ended.

recap.keyIdea: Ask how the head of government is chosen and who can remove them: a legislature that can remove them marks a parliamentary system, a separate election with no such power marks a presidential one, and a president beside a prime minister who answers to the legislature marks a semi-presidential one.

blocks.text: In a parliamentary system the head of government depends on the confidence of a majority of parliament. In a presidential system citizens elect them and the legislature can dismiss them only in extraordinary cases. A semi-presidential system has both a president and a prime minister, and the cabinet answers to the legislature, which can force it out.

Titles don't settle any of this, since dictators and leaders of one-party states often carry the title of president. The same questions also say how fused or separated the executive and the legislature are, and the writers who argue about it, Montesquieu, Bagehot and Wilson, each point to something different that a constitution should protect.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the courts and asks what a court can do when a law or an act of the executive breaks the constitution.

lessons.title: What courts can and cannot do
lessons.orientation: Judge what a court can do about an act of the legislature or the executive in a described case, using Hamilton's argument and the three approaches to review.
lessons.reviewLabel: What courts can and cannot do
lessons.nextAction: Say what an electoral system does to a party's share of the seats compared with its share of the votes.

blocks.text: When a court strikes down a law, it can look like the most powerful body in the country: a handful of judges undoing what an elected legislature has voted for. Yet Alexander Hamilton, writing in 1788 to win support for the new American Constitution, called the judiciary the weakest of the three branches, and the same essay lays the groundwork for courts to strike laws down.

Both things can hold at once, because deciding that a law breaks the constitution is one thing and making the decision stick is another. Where a court's power ends, and how differently countries have drawn that line, decides what a ruling in the news means.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a court can and can't do about a law or an official's decision.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether a court can overturn a law varies between democracies, so a news story about a ruling makes sense only once you know which arrangement the country has.

recap.keyIdea: A court decides whether an act of the executive or the legislature is lawful, with no force or will of its own, and how far it can go with a statute depends on the arrangement its country has chosen.

blocks.text: Hamilton called the judiciary the weakest branch because it commands neither the sword nor the purse and depends on the executive to carry out its judgments. His case for review rests on the power of the people standing above both courts and legislature, so a judge who follows the constitution over a conflicting statute is following the higher of two laws.

Countries answer the question about statutes in three ways: no review, review by the ordinary courts, or review by a constitutional court, and the United Kingdom's declaration of incompatibility is a variation on the first. Review of an official's decision is a separate matter, because the court asks whether the decision was lawful and usually leaves the decision itself where it was.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from courts to elections, and asks what an electoral system does to the votes that go into it.

lead.text: Hamilton's reason for calling the judiciary the weakest branch is a short inventory of what it lacks. The sword stands for a society's strength and the purse for its wealth, and the courts, he says, direct neither. They can take no active resolution of their own, so they have "neither FORCE nor WILL" and only judgment, and in the end they depend on the executive arm to give their judgments any effect.

That picture of a judge has an older source. Montesquieu, whose account of the separation of powers we met earlier, called the national judges "no more than the mouth" that speaks the law, "mere passive beings" who cannot soften its force or rigor. His judges apply the law as it stands and have no say in what it is. Hamilton accepts that courts have no force and no will, and then argues that they have a duty Montesquieu's judges lack. The next screens follow that argument.

reveal.text: The following screens show why Hamilton thinks that testing a law against the constitution belongs to judges.

lead.text: If judges have no force of their own, they have to be protected from the branches that do, because those branches could punish a judge for a ruling they dislike. Hamilton called the remedy one of the best modern improvements in the practice of government: judges who keep their office for as long as they behave well. Under a monarch, he said, that tenure protects against the prince's despotism, and in a republic it protects just as well against the legislature's encroachments and oppressions.

The constitutions of the United States and Australia do the same, with a difference. The United States Constitution lets judges keep their offices for as long as they behave well and bars any reduction of their compensation while they serve. In Australia a justice can be removed only when both Houses of Parliament ask the Governor-General in Council to do so, and only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and Parliament fixes the pay but cannot reduce it while a justice serves. We call this protection **judicial independence**: tenure that outlasts any one unpopular ruling, and pay that cannot be cut in reply to one.

Start with the term. In a **judicial review**, a court examines whether something a government has done is lawful, whether that is an official's decision or, in some countries, a statute. Hamilton makes the case for the most contested kind, a court setting aside a statute that conflicts with the constitution, and he builds it in five links.

The first link says that limits on a legislature last only if courts can declare acts against them void. The second borrows a rule about agents: whatever someone does against the commission under which they act is void, since to say otherwise would put the deputy above the principal and the representatives of the people above the people. The third says the interpretation of laws belongs to the courts and that a constitution is a fundamental law. The fourth is where the weight falls, because the power of the people stands above both the courts and the legislature, and the fifth is the conclusion.

afterFigure.text: Hamilton knew the obvious objection, that judges might put their own pleasure in place of the legislature's and call it a conflict with the constitution. He answers that the same thing could happen with two contradictory statutes, or in judging any single statute, since the courts' task is to say what the law means, and a judge who uses will in place of judgment would swap the legislature's pleasure for their own wherever the case arose. For him the danger lies in bad judging, and he does not accept that it tells against review in particular.

The argument came before the text. The text of the United States Constitution never gave federal courts that power in so many words, and the Supreme Court took the step in *Marbury v. Madison*, argued in 1803, fifteen years after Hamilton's essay.

lead.text: Hamilton argued for review in one country, and other countries have arranged it differently, so the first thing to find out about any ruling is which arrangement its country has. The Wikipedia article on judicial review describes three.

In the first, courts have no power to strike down statutes. British judges cannot strike down an Act of Parliament, because of a strong attachment to the idea that the legislature is supreme, and the Dutch constitution expressly bars courts from ruling on whether a statute is constitutional. In the second, the ordinary courts do the reviewing. Countries that inherited the English common law system, among them Australia, Canada and the United States, generally leave review to courts of general jurisdiction, and in India the Supreme Court and the state High Courts can invalidate legislation that goes against the constitution, particularly where it infringes fundamental rights.

In the third, one court does the reviewing. In 1920 Czechoslovakia adopted review by a specialised **constitutional court**, a design written by the jurist Hans Kelsen, and Austria adopted it at the same time. In these systems the other courts cannot question a statute's constitutionality, although they often may start the process of review by sending the question on. Germany has a dedicated constitutional court that does this work and no other.

reveal.text: Two descriptions fit each approach, so asking who may rule on a statute sorts any country into one of the three.

lead.text: The United Kingdom has a variation on the first approach. The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into British law, and with it courts were given the power to issue a **declaration of incompatibility** when they find legislation inconsistent with the Convention. Such a declaration does not disapply the statute. It works as a request to Parliament to put the breach right through the legislative process.

That leaves legislative supremacy standing, since Parliament decides what happens to its own Act, and it still lets a court say plainly that the Act clashes with rights the country has accepted. So the declaration tells Parliament something, and what changes next is left to Parliament.

Most reviews in daily life concern something smaller than a statute, such as a decision by an official or a public body. The same article stresses that reviewing an administrative act is a different thing from hearing an appeal. In a review the court does not usually take the decision over. It asks whether the official's decision followed the law and principles such as fair procedure and the legitimate expectations of the person affected.

That echoes Hamilton's line between will and judgment. A court that asked whether it would have decided the same way would be exercising its own will, and a court that asks whether the official followed the law is exercising judgment.

steps.headline: An official refuses someone a residence permit, and the applicant asks a court to review the refusal. What does the court ask?

lead.text: Take the steps in order, and notice where the court stops.

workedSteps.text: Start with what is being challenged. It is an official's decision, and no statute is in question, so this is a review of an administrative act and the question is about the decision's lawfulness.
The court asks whether the official followed the law that governs the decision and the principles of fair procedure.
The court does not usually take the decision over, so whether the judge would have decided the same way is not the test.
An applicant who wins has shown that the decision did not comply with the law or with fair procedure. A claim that the decision was harsh or unwise is a different kind of claim.

reveal.text: Reading a report of a ruling starts with who may rule on a statute in that country.

lessons.title: From votes to seats
lessons.orientation: Say what an electoral system does to the votes that go into it: who gains, which way the seat share moves and why, from plurality and the proportional methods to a constitution's own seat rule.
lessons.nextAction: Read Madison's argument about factions as a chain of claims and apply it to a case.

blocks.text: In the UK's 2024 general election Reform UK took 14.3 percent of the votes cast, the third-largest share, yet won only 5 seats, which is 0.7 percent of Parliament. The Liberal Democrats took 12.2 percent, fewer votes than Reform UK, and won 72 seats. A party with fewer votes ended up with far more seats, which couldn't happen if seats simply followed votes.

So the rule that turns votes into seats must be doing something of its own, and countries have chosen rules that do quite different things with the same votes. Which party gains, and by how much, depends on the rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say who gains and who loses from the way a system turns votes into seats.
intro.whyItMatters: News about a surprising election result usually turns on the rule that counted the votes, and the rule decides which parties benefit.

recap.keyIdea: An electoral system decides how votes become seats, so the same votes can give different results: plurality in districts rewards concentrated support, proportional methods follow votes more closely, and the Gallagher index measures the gap.

blocks.text: Under first past the post each district elects the candidate with a plurality, so a party's seats depend on where its votes are as well as how many it has. That is how a party can win a majority of seats with a minority of the votes, or fewer seats than a party with fewer votes.

Proportional rules share seats by divisors, as D'Hondt does, or by quotas, as largest remainder does with the Hare quota, and the Droop quota fixes how much of a district's vote guarantees a seat. The methods give different seats from the same votes, with D'Hondt favouring larger parties, and the Gallagher index puts a number on how far any one result sits from proportional. Whether to prefer majority governments or closer proportionality is a matter on which people disagree.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from how votes become seats to the groups that compete for them, and asks what Madison made of a faction.

lead.text: Start with the rule behind the British result. Under **first past the post**, each district elects one member, and the candidate who gets more first-choice votes than anyone else wins, even without more than half of all the votes. Having more votes than any rival, even without a majority, is called a **plurality**. The runner-up's votes then add nothing to the result in that district, and neither do the winner's votes beyond what was needed to win. The Wikipedia article on the rule gives an example, a vote on where Tennessee's capital should be. Memphis takes 42 percent of first choices, Nashville 26, Knoxville 17 and Chattanooga 15, so Memphis wins, although it sits far from the centre of the state and most voters would rather have Nashville than any one of the others.

To see what happens across a whole country, take an invented one with five districts of 10,000 votes each and three parties, X, Y and Z. Party X wins three districts narrowly, with 4,600 votes to Y's 4,400, and Y wins the other two by a landslide, 7,500 to 1,500. Add up the districts and Y has 28,200 of the 50,000 votes, which is 56.4 percent, against X's 33.6 percent and Z's 10, but X holds three of the five seats and Y only two. Z comes third everywhere and has none.

afterFigure.text: Y piled up its votes in two districts, where 7,500 was far more than it needed, and fell narrowly short in the other three. The article calls the votes cast for losing candidates, and the excess votes for winners, **wasted votes**, and it gives the British general election of 2005 as an example: 52 percent of votes went to losing candidates and 18 percent were excess votes, a total of 70 percent. The general effect, the article says, is that big parties and parties whose voters are clustered in particular places collect more seats than their votes warrant, while small parties and parties with evenly spread voters collect fewer.

reveal.text: Plurality rewards a lead in a district, whatever the national share. The next screens show rules that count votes across the whole country instead.

lead.text: **Proportional representation** is the name for rules that share seats among parties according to their share of the votes. Exact proportionality is never achieved under them except by chance, since seats come in whole numbers and the rules differ in how they round. The first we'll meet is the **D'Hondt method**, described in 1792 by Thomas Jefferson and re-invented independently in 1878 by the Belgian lawyer Victor D'Hondt, which is why it has two names.

Its procedure is simple to state. Divide each party's total votes by one, then by two, then three and so on, build a grid of the results, and give seats to the highest numbers in the whole grid, as many as there are seats. Suppose eight seats are to be shared among our three parties. Y's 28,200 is the biggest number, so Y wins the first seat, then X's 16,800, then Y's 14,100, Y's 9,400, X's 8,400, Y's 7,050, Y's 5,640 and X's 5,600. That makes five for Y, three for X and none for Z. Z's 5,000 is the next number in line, only 600 short of the last winner, but it comes too late.

afterFigure.text: Seat shares are now 62.5 percent for Y and 37.5 for X, against vote shares of 56.4 and 33.6, and the smallest party has nothing despite a tenth of the votes. The article says that D'Hondt tilts towards large parties and coalitions at the expense of small ones, and that on other measures it is among the least proportional of the proportional methods. One invented election doesn't prove that, but it shows the direction.

diagram.caption: Eight seats shared by D'Hondt. The eight highlighted numbers are the highest in the grid, so Y wins five seats, X three and Z none.

lead.text: A second family of rules shares seats using a quota. Divide the valid votes by the number of seats and you have the **Hare quota**. Divide each party's votes by it, give each party the whole number of seats in its result, and the seats still unfilled go to the parties with the largest fractional remainders. That last step is what gives the **largest remainder method** its name.

In our invented country the Hare quota is 50,000 divided by 8, which is 6,250 votes. X's 16,800 votes come to 2.69 quotas, Y's 28,200 to 4.51 and Z's 5,000 to 0.80. The whole numbers give X two seats, Y four and Z none, which fills six, and the two seats left go to the largest remainders, Z's 0.80 and X's 0.69. The result is three seats for X, four for Y and one for Z.

afterFigure.text: Z, which got nothing under D'Hondt, gets a seat here, and Y gives one up for it. The article says the Hare quota treats parties of different sizes even-handedly and is kinder to less popular parties than the quota we meet next, and it names Hong Kong, Brazil and Guyana as places that use it with largest remainder. So "proportional" names a family of rules, and two of them can give different seats from the same votes.

diagram.alt: A table for largest remainder with the Hare quota of 6,250 votes: votes, votes divided by the quota, whole seats, remainder and final seats for X, Y and Z. A second view compares the seats each party wins under plurality, D'Hondt and largest remainder.
diagram.caption: The quota method for eight seats, and then the three methods' seats side by side. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: One election doesn't prove a rule, but here the pattern matches what the articles say about each method.

lead.text: A third quota works inside one district. The **Droop quota** names how many votes make a seat certain for a party or candidate in a district. For k seats it is the total votes divided by k plus one, which as a share of the vote is $\frac{1}{k+1}$, so in a three-seat district any candidate above 25 percent is sure of election. It is used with the single transferable vote, where voters rank candidates and a winner's excess votes pass to their next choices. In the article's example of 100 votes and three seats the quota is 25, so a candidate with 45 votes is elected at once, and the 20 excess votes pass to the voters' next choices.

Because the share is $\frac{1}{k+1}$, the more seats a district has, the smaller the share that guarantees one. Malta uses the single transferable vote in five-member districts, where successful candidates commonly receive 16.6 percent of the district's vote, and the article says the country keeps a very strong two-party system. New South Wales elects its legislative council in 21-seat contests, where about 1/22nd of the vote takes a seat, and seven or eight different parties win seats each time.

Droop and Hare also differ in who they favour. Because it is smaller than the Hare quota, more parties can win a second seat or more under it, and the article calls it biased towards large parties. On the other side, a party with a majority of a district's votes is sure of at least half its seats under Droop, which Hare doesn't always guarantee.

To say how far a result is from proportional, political scientists use the **Gallagher index**. For each party you take the difference between its percentage of the votes and its percentage of the seats and square it, add the squares for every party, halve the sum and take the square root. The division by two keeps the index between 0 and 100, and the larger the gaps, the larger the index, with 0 for a perfectly proportional result.

For our invented country the index is 23.1 under plurality, 8.7 under D'Hondt and 5.6 under largest remainder with the Hare quota. The bars show why: as you switch between the three, the seat bars move toward the vote bars.

afterFigure.text: Real elections give the same kind of spread. The index was 12.02 for Canada's 2015 federal election, held under plurality, and a Canadian parliamentary committee in 2016 recommended that any new system aim for a Gallagher score of 5 or less, a level the article says is consistently reached in European proportional systems. Sweden's 2022 election scored 0.64 under the modified Sainte-Laguë method, Ireland's 2020 election 1.96 under the single transferable vote with the Droop quota, and Queensland's 2012 election 31.16, after a landslide in which the LNP won 88 percent of the seats with less than 50 percent of the vote. The index measures the gap in a single election, and by itself it says nothing about why the gap arose or what anyone should do about it.

lead.text: A constitution can write the seat rule into its own text. Section 7 of Australia's Constitution Act gives each Original State six senators until Parliament provides otherwise, and section 24 says the House of Representatives shall have, as nearly as practicable, twice as many members as the Senate has senators. The Commonwealth's people are divided by twice the number of senators to give a quota, each State's people are divided by that quota, and a State gets one more member if the remainder is greater than half a quota. A final clause sets a floor of five members for each Original State.

Take six invented States, not Australia's, with 36 senators between them, so that twice the senators is 72, and a population of 3,600,000, so that the quota is 50,000. The largest State, with 1,080,000 people, comes to 21.6 quotas, and a remainder of 30,000 is more than half a quota, so it gets 22 members. The smallest, with 140,000, comes to 2.8 quotas and would get 3, but the floor lifts it to 5. The six States get 22, 20, 12, 10, 6 and 5, which makes a House of 75.

afterFigure.text: The floor changes who counts for how much. The smallest State has 3.9 percent of the people and, with five members, 6.7 percent of the House, so the floor lifts its share of the House above its share of the people.

diagram.alt: A table of six invented States with their populations, the number of quotas each contains, the members the quota rule gives, and the members after the floor of five. State F's 140,000 people give 3 members by the rule and 5 with the floor, and the House totals 75.

lead.text: People who study electoral systems disagree about which results matter. Supporters of first past the post cite its ability to produce majority governments, and they argue that under proportional representation small parties may act as kingmakers in coalitions, so that their say over policy outstrips their size. Supporters of proportional representation reply that coalitions are an advantage, because they force compromise towards the centre of the political spectrum. Opponents of proportional representation answer that two-party plurality avoids those problems: coalitions are rare, the two big parties compete at the centre, a strong opposition is assured, and governments are regularly voted out.

John Stuart Mill, whose Considerations on Representative Government appeared in 1861, endorsed proportional representation by the single transferable vote that Thomas Hare had proposed. For Mill, democracy as commonly practised is government by "a mere majority", and without adequate representation of minorities he calls it "a false show of democracy". These positions weigh different things, majority government and a strong opposition on one side and minority representation and compromise on the other, and we won't choose between them here.

reveal.text: The two sides describe the same bargaining and judge it in opposite ways, so the disagreement is about values and no count of votes can settle it.

lessons.title: Factions, parties and interest groups
lessons.orientation: Read Madison's argument in Federalist 10 as a chain of claims and apply it to a case, and tell a party, an interest group and a faction inside a party apart by what each is for.
lessons.nextAction: Say where an event sits in the policy cycle and what a simple budget shows.

blocks.text: Free people form groups around a shared passion or interest, and some of those groups pursue it against the rights of other citizens or against the interests of the community as a whole. In Federalist No. 10, published on 22 November 1787, James Madison asked what a constitution could do about a group like that.
His problem was how to protect a minority from a majority with a common interest against it, without destroying the liberty that lets such groups form in the first place.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow Madison's argument and tell a party, an interest group and a faction inside a party apart.
intro.whyItMatters: Parties, lobbies and factions all compete for influence in different ways, and you need to know which one you're looking at to judge what it can do.

recap.keyIdea: Madison treats faction as a danger that can't be removed without destroying liberty, so he looks to controlling its effects, and a party, an interest group and a faction inside a party are told apart by what each is for.

blocks.text: Madison defines a faction as any group, majority or minority, drawn together by a passion or interest against the rights of others or the interests of the community. Its causes lie in liberty and in the unequal distribution of property, so he looks to controlling its effects: a minority faction is defeated by the vote, a pure democracy has no remedy against a majority one, and a republic spread over a large sphere makes a majority with a common motive less probable.

A party is focused on electing candidates and an interest group on advancing a policy agenda, while a faction in the newspaper sense is a subgroup within a party. Interest groups face the free rider problem, parties exist in autocracies as well as democracies, and Duverger's law links plurality voting to two-party systems, a pattern that is heavily debated.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows what happens after parties and groups have done their work, and asks how public opinion turns into policy and a budget.

lead.text: Madison calls such a group a **faction**. It is any set of citizens, whether it holds a majority or only a minority, who are drawn together by a shared passion or interest and who act against the rights of other citizens or the lasting interests of the community. Size isn't part of the definition: a group counts as a faction because of what it does to others, whether it is large or small.

He saw two ways to cure the harm that factions do. One is to remove their causes and the other is to control their effects. The first, he thought, was a cure worse than the disease. His image is that liberty feeds faction as air feeds fire, and abolishing liberty to stop faction would be as foolish as abolishing air to stop fire. The causes also lie deep in human affairs, since in his view the most common and lasting source of faction has been the unequal distribution of property, with owners and the propertyless forming separate interests. So the causes can't be removed, and the remedy has to be found in controlling the effects.

The word has a second meaning. A newspaper that writes of a party's left-wing faction means a subgroup inside the party, which is also how the Wikipedia article on political parties uses it. Madison's faction is wider than that, so it helps to keep the two meanings apart.

reveal.text: Keep the two meanings apart: a faction in Madison's sense is judged by its effect on others, and in the newspaper's sense by where it sits inside a party.

lead.text: Madison's remedy has to work against two kinds of faction. A faction in the minority is the easier case, because the republican principle lets the majority defeat it by an ordinary vote. Such a group may clog the administration or convulse the society, he allows, but it can't carry out and disguise its violence behind constitutional forms.

A faction that is a majority is the hard case. Madison defines a **pure democracy** as a society small enough for its citizens to assemble and run the government in person, and he concludes that it has no cure for the harm of faction. Shared passions or interests will almost always be felt by a majority there, the form of government itself lets them communicate and act together, and nothing checks the temptation to sacrifice the weaker party.

The town of 400 in the opening question is a pure democracy in Madison's sense: every adult votes at one meeting, and a majority that wants to tax the minority needs nothing more than the vote it already holds.

Madison's answer is the **republic**, a government that works by representation. He lists two differences from a pure democracy: the government is placed in the hands of a few citizens chosen by the rest, and a republic can cover more citizens and a wider territory.

The second difference carries the argument. Widen the sphere, he says, and you take in more kinds of parties and interests, so it becomes less likely that a majority of the whole will share a motive for invading the rights of others. If such a motive does exist, those who feel it will find it harder to discover their strength and to act together.

afterFigure.text: Madison doesn't claim to remove faction: a republic leaves the groups in place and makes it harder for a majority among them to form and act together.

diagram.alt: A tree of Madison's argument. Faction can be cured by removing its causes, which would mean abolishing liberty and is worse than the disease, or by controlling its effects. A second view shows how: a minority faction is outvoted, and a majority faction is made harder to form by a large republic.
diagram.caption: Madison's two methods and what follows from each. Use the buttons to add the second half.

lead.text: Madison's faction is a wider idea than a party. The Wikipedia article on political parties defines a **political party** as an organisation that puts up candidates to compete in elections and takes part in governing. It separates four things that people often run together: a party concentrates on electing candidates, a parliamentary group is a group of parties, a faction is a subgroup within a party, and an advocacy group concentrates on advancing a policy agenda.

Advocacy groups, which the article also calls **interest groups**, lobby groups or pressure groups, try to influence public opinion and, in the end, public policy. So the test that tells these organisations apart is their aim, and the label a group gives itself matters much less.

reveal.text: Two organisations can want the same policy and still differ in kind, since one puts up candidates and the other doesn't.

lead.text: One general theory says that people join an interest group only if something tempts them to. The **free rider problem** is the difficulty that arises when the benefits go to everyone, member or not. A group campaigning for better farming standards, for example, works for every farmer, including those who never joined, so a farmer can enjoy the result without paying dues.

A second idea in the article is **pluralism**, the view that advocacy groups compete with one another and play a part in the political system by acting as a counterweight to concentrations of power. It echoes Madison's argument for variety: when many interests compete, none is likely to rule alone.

Parties matter in autocracies as well as democracies, though democracies usually have more of them, and an autocracy often has one governing party. In a one-party system a single party holds all the power. Some autocracies ban parties altogether, and in Saudi Arabia the ban has been used to protect the monarchy.

Among democracies the number of parties often seems to depend on the electoral rule, which links this lesson to the last. In the 1950s Maurice Duverger observed that plurality elections in single-member districts tend to produce two-party systems, and the observation came to be called **Duverger's law**. Whether the pattern holds has been heavily debated for decades. Several of the biggest democracies, among them India, Indonesia, Pakistan and Brazil, have had long periods of competition among many parties.

reveal.text: Madison offers a cure for the mischief of a majority faction, and he describes it as making that mischief less probable.

lessons.title: From public opinion to policy and budget
lessons.orientation: Place a described event at its stage in the policy cycle and say who acts there, read a simple government budget as receipts, spending and balance, and say what a poll can and cannot show about public opinion.
lessons.reviewLabel: From public opinion to policy and budget
lessons.nextAction: Apply Mill's principle to a law, and say whom a rights clause restrains.

blocks.text: Governments watch what people say they think, through polls, newspapers, petitions and protests, and then they decide things: laws, regulations and, above all, how to spend public money. Between what people think and what a government does lie several steps, each with its own actors, and at each of them something can be lost.
We'll follow that path from opinion to policy and then to the budget, and ask where it can break. It starts with a question about what a poll can tell us at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place an event in the policy cycle and read a simple budget.
intro.whyItMatters: A law that nobody pays for or carries out changes nothing, so the cycle and the budget show where good intentions get stuck.

recap.keyIdea: Opinion reaches policy through a cycle of agenda setting, formulation, legitimation, implementation and evaluation, and a budget decides whether a law gets the money to be carried out.

blocks.text: Polls measure opinion, and framing and agenda setting shape what people think, while people asked about something unfamiliar often give answers meant to please. Opinion and policy influence each other, and the policy cycle runs from agenda setting through formulation, legitimation and implementation to an evaluation that can send an issue back to the start.

A budget projects receipts and spending, and it is in deficit when spending is larger, which is usually financed by borrowing. It doesn't release money on its own, since constitutions require an appropriation made by law, and officials then carry the policy out, which is where the gap between goals on paper and results in practice can open.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to rights, and asks what limits a majority and the government that serves it should meet.

lead.text: **Public opinion** is the collective opinion on a topic or a voting intention that is relevant to society, the people's views on matters that affect them. The Wikipedia article on it says opinion can be obtained accurately through survey sampling, and it also gives reasons to read a poll with care.

It names three ways that opinion forms and shifts. Major media outlets set the agenda, deciding what is newsworthy and when it will be reported, which is called **agenda setting**. They also practise **framing**, presenting a story in a particular way to sway the audience's attitude. And people asked about a subject they know little about often give a **pseudo-opinion**, an answer they think will please whoever is asking. So the figure from a poll depends partly on what people have been told and how they were asked.

reveal.text: Opinion is shaped by how a story is told as well as by whether it is told, and the next screens follow what a government does with it.

lead.text: **Public policy** covers what a government does about social problems: its laws, its regulations, its guidelines and the other actions it takes or proposes. The Wikipedia article on public policy describes a basic sequence of five stages, a **policy cycle**, and adds that writers draw the stages in different ways.

It starts with agenda setting, which identifies the problems that need government attention, decides which deserve the most and defines what kind of problem each is. Formulation sets out the objectives and works out the costs and effects of the solutions that could be proposed. **Legitimation** gathers approval, whether from the executive, the legislature, a consultation or a referendum. Implementation sets up or uses an organisation to take responsibility, gives it the resources and legal authority to act, and checks that the policy is carried out as planned. Evaluation assesses how far the policy has succeeded and whether it was the right policy in the first place.

afterFigure.text: The cycle isn't a one-way street. An evaluation can send an issue back to the agenda, which is the dotted arrow. The article adds that influence between opinion and policy runs both ways: opinion can move policy, and what people receive from a policy shapes what they come to expect and think.

diagram.alt: A cycle of five boxes: agenda setting, formulation, legitimation, implementation and evaluation, joined by arrows, with a dotted arrow from evaluation back to agenda setting.

lead.text: A **government budget** projects what the government expects to collect and spend over a period, usually a financial year, which need not match the calendar year. A budget is a plan: on its own it doesn't release any money, because spending needs a further law.

Both constitutions we've read put the legislature in charge of the money. In each, money can leave the Treasury only under an appropriation made by law, and the United States Constitution adds that a regular account of receipts and expenditures must be published. Bills for raising revenue must start in the House of Representatives in the United States, and in Australia a bill that taxes or appropriates may not start in the Senate.

Every budget has two sides. Revenues come mostly from taxes, such as income, sales, property or corporate tax, and from fees and charges, which are payments for services the government provides: charges for issuing permits, fees for sewage treatment, even fines for breaking laws. Expenses include what economists call government consumption, meaning spending on current goods and services, together with investment such as infrastructure or research and transfer payments such as unemployment or retirement benefits.

Compare the two totals and the budget is in one of three states. It is balanced when receipts equal expenditure, in surplus when receipts exceed it, and in **deficit** when expenditure exceeds receipts, and governments usually finance a deficit by borrowing from private lenders at home, from other governments or from international institutions. In the invented budget in the figure, receipts come to 650 million and spending to 670 million, so the budget is in deficit.

afterFigure.text: Taxes provide 570 of the 650 million here, which fits what the article says about most governments, and the 20 million gap is what has to be financed by borrowing. The figures are invented.

lead.text: Between a law and its effect stand the officials who carry it out. In Max Weber's view, as the Wikipedia article on bureaucracy reports it, **bureaucracy** is the most efficient and rational way to organise large-scale human activity, since systematic processes and organised hierarchies keep order, raise efficiency and remove favouritism. He also warned that unchecked bureaucracy endangers individual freedom, because it can trap people in an impersonal "iron cage" of rules.

The article names two dilemmas. One is how independent officials should be of the politicians they serve, since they might answer to them directly or hold some autonomy. The other is how closely they must follow set rules, and how much room they should have to find solutions where no rule foresaw the case. The article uses the name **implementation gap** for the difference between policy goals on paper and implementation in practice.

reveal.text: A cost in a published budget and money that can be spent are different things, as the constitutions' rule about appropriations shows.

lessons.title: Rights and the majority

lead.text: John Stuart Mill's essay *On Liberty*, published in 1859, begins with a worry about majorities. The oppression of individuals or of a minority by a ruling majority is called the **tyranny of the majority**, and Mill says it was first dreaded, and is still commonly dreaded, mainly as something done through the acts of public authorities. On that view the danger is a government that does the majority's bidding through laws and penalties.

Reflective people, he says, saw a further danger. When society is itself the tyrant, ruling over the separate individuals who make it up, it isn't limited to acting through officials. It can issue its own mandates, and if those mandates are wrong, or reach into things society ought not to meddle with, it practises a **social tyranny**. Mill thought this *more* formidable than many political oppressions. Its penalties are usually less extreme, but it leaves fewer ways to escape, reaches much deeper into the details of life and, in his words, enslaves "the soul itself".

That is why he concludes that protection against the magistrate is not enough: people also need protection against the opinion and feeling that prevail around them. The next screen gives the principle he offers against both.

Against that background Mill states the one principle his essay defends. It covers every way a community can press on one of its members, whether by physical force, such as legal penalties, or by the moral coercion of public opinion. He claims that the only thing that warrants interfering with any member's liberty of action, by one person or by the whole community, is self-protection. In other words, **power may rightfully be used against a member of a community, against his will, only to prevent harm to others**. We'll call this Mill's principle.

The principle also rules something out. A person's own good, physical or moral, isn't a *sufficient* warrant. Mill says no one can rightfully be compelled to do something, or to hold back from it, because it would be better for him, because it would make him happier, or because other people think it wise or even right. Those are good reasons for reasoning with him, pleading with him and trying to persuade him, but they don't justify compelling him or making him suffer for refusing.

What is left over belongs to the person. The only part of anyone's conduct for which he answers to society, Mill says, is the part that concerns others. In the part that concerns only himself his independence is absolute, and he describes the individual as sovereign over his own body and mind.

afterFigure.text: The figure lays the principle along a line. At the left end society may argue, plead and persuade but may not compel, and at the right end, where one person's conduct harms another, it may. So a law that stops one person harming another passes the test, and a law that stops someone harming only himself, or that rests only on what other people think wise, doesn't.

A second view adds what society may do at each end.

lead.text: Apply Mill's principle to six invented laws, asking of each whether anyone other than the person it restricts is harmed.

reveal.text: Three of the laws prevent harm to other people, so the principle allows them. The other three restrict a person's own conduct, or punish what the majority merely dislikes, and the principle gives the state no warrant for those.

lead.text: Tocqueville came to the same worry from a visit to the United States. He and Beaumont were sent to the United States in 1831 by the French government to study its prisons, and they spent nine months there. In the first volume of *Democracy in America*, published in 1835, he puts a puzzle to himself. He holds that all authority begins in the will of the majority, and he also calls it an impious and execrable maxim that, in politics, a people has a right to do whatever it pleases. Is he contradicting himself?

His answer starts from a comparison. Take the majority as a whole and think of it as one being whose opinions and, most often, whose interests clash with those of another being, the minority. We already accept that a man with absolute power can misuse it by wronging his adversaries, so why, he asks, should a majority not be open to the same reproach?

The comparison removes an assumption that is easy to make, that a majority is safe because it is the majority. A majority has *opponents*, and its power can be turned against them as a monarch's can. Mill and Tocqueville both use the phrase tyranny of the majority for that danger, though as we'll see they stress different things.

reveal.text: Tocqueville's comparison makes the majority an actor with opponents, so its size shows who holds the power and says nothing about whether the power is used fairly.

lead.text: So far the majority has acted through laws and officials, and both writers say it can act without them. Tocqueville contrasts it with a king, whose authority, he says, is purely physical: it controls what a subject does without subduing what he privately wills. The majority has a power that is physical and moral at once, and it acts on **the will as well as on the actions** of men. It represses open contest and all controversy, and of America he says that he knows of no country where minds are less independent and discussion less free.

That claim sits close to Mill's. Mill says society's mandates reach much deeper into the details of life than political penalties do, and Tocqueville says the majority reaches the will itself. Mill's emphasis falls on society's own mandates and how far they reach, and Tocqueville's on the majority's power to suppress contest and controversy. Neither needs a statute.

Tocqueville then hedges. He does not claim that tyrannical abuses are frequent in America at the time he writes. He says that no sure barrier has been set up against them, and that what keeps the government mild owes more to the circumstances and manners of the country than to its laws. A mildness that depends on circumstances and manners is a different thing from a safeguard written into law, and his point is that America, in his view, had the first and not the second.

reveal.text: Mill's principle names both means in its first sentence, legal penalties and the moral coercion of public opinion, so a case with no law in it can still be a case of coercion.

lead.text: One response to the danger is to write protections down. Wikipedia's article on democracy says that without something to compensate for it, such as legal protections of individual or group rights, the tyranny of the majority can oppress political minorities. A protection has to say whom it binds, so the wording of a clause matters. Wikipedia's article on civil liberties describes **civil liberties** as the fundamental rights and freedoms that governments promise not to limit, without due process of law, whether by a constitution, a statute or a court's interpretation. So a civil liberty is first of all a promise made by the government.

Three clauses from the Bill of Rights as it was proposed in 1789 show how much the wording matters. The clause that became the First Amendment begins with its target: Congress shall make no law establishing a religion, forbidding its free practice, restricting speech or the press, or limiting the right of the people to assemble peaceably and to petition the government. It restrains the body that makes laws, and it doesn't mention newspapers, employers or neighbours, so as written it places no duty on them.

The other two clauses are worded differently. One protects people's security in their persons, homes, papers and belongings against unreasonable searches and seizures, and says that warrants may issue only on probable cause, backed by an oath or affirmation, and must say precisely which place is to be searched and which persons or things are to be seized. The other says that no one is to be compelled in a criminal case to testify against himself, or to lose life, liberty or property unless due process of law is followed. Neither names who must not act. Each limits an act instead, searching and seizing, or compelling and depriving.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts the three side by side. Its last column lists what each text leaves open, such as what makes a search unreasonable and what process is due, and a clause can't be applied without an answer to those questions.

reveal.text: The clause's first words name its target. Reading a rights text starts with who is told what they shall not do, and this clause answers that by naming Congress.

lead.text: Rights texts face a further problem when the state is in danger. Wikipedia's article on civil liberties says that suspending or altering some civil liberties in wartime or in a **state of emergency** is a matter of debate, including whether it should happen and how far. Its article on constitutions adds that many constitutions allow a government to declare, in exceptional circumstances, a state of emergency in which some rights and guarantees are set aside, and that governments have abused the provision, and could again, to suppress dissent and disregard human rights.

Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, meets the difficulty from the other side. It allows limits on rights, but only limits fixed by law, and only to secure the rights of others and to meet what a democratic society fairly requires for morality, public order and the general welfare. Mill's principle names one ground, harm to others. The declaration names several, so its list is longer.

Between them the two give us questions to ask of any limit on rights, an emergency measure included. Is the limit fixed by law? Does its purpose fit what the principle or the declaration allows? Neither text says how to answer them in a hard case.

reveal.text: A power that suspends rights is dangerous in the hands of a government that wants to silence its critics, and the extract's warning is about exactly that.

lead.text: Mill's principle tells a lawmaker what kind of reason a law needs, which is harm to others. It doesn't say what counts as harm, and people who accept the principle can disagree about that. The next case is one where they might.

reveal.text: The principle fixes the test. Whether giving offence counts as harm is a further question, and it is where people who share Mill's principle can still disagree.

lessons.orientation: Apply Mill's principle on liberty to a described law and say whether it passes his test, use Tocqueville to name a way a majority can limit liberty without any law, and read who a rights clause restrains.
lessons.nextAction: Say whether a state is federal or unitary, which level holds a power, and who can change the division.

blocks.text: Suppose the voters of a town, in a fair election and by a large margin, ban a small political group from meeting in the town hall. Everyone had a say, and most of them agreed. Does that settle whether the ban is justified?

Two nineteenth-century writers, John Stuart Mill and Alexis de Tocqueville, both worried about exactly this: a majority can use its power against the people who lost the vote. Their arguments give us a test to put to a law and a way to read what a bill of rights does and doesn't restrain.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to test a law against Mill's principle, name the pressure a majority can apply with no law at all, and say whom a rights clause restrains.
intro.whyItMatters: A law can pass by a large majority and still limit someone's liberty, so you need tests that don't depend on how many people voted for it.

recap.keyIdea: Mill allows compelling a person only to prevent harm to others, a majority can press on people's minds without any law, and a rights clause restrains whoever its wording names.

blocks.text: Mill's principle allows power over a person against his will only to prevent harm to others, and it says a person's own good is not enough. He adds that the pressure of prevailing opinion can be a tyranny more formidable than many political ones, and Tocqueville says the majority acts on the will as well as the actions, while also saying that he does not claim abuses are frequent and that no sure barrier stands against them.

A rights clause limits whoever its wording names, as "Congress shall make no law" limits the lawmaker, and some clauses limit an act without naming anyone. Wikipedia's article on constitutions says emergency provisions can be and have been abused to suppress dissent, and Mill's principle leaves open what counts as harm.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the rights of individuals to the levels of government, and asks who can change the division of powers between a national government and its regions.

lessons.title: Federal and unitary states

lead.text: A **federal** state combines a central government with a regional level of governments, such as states, provinces, cantons or territories, and divides the powers of governing between the two. A **unitary** state is run as a single unit, with the central government as the supreme authority. It can create or abolish administrative divisions, and those divisions exercise only the powers it chooses to delegate.

A unitary state can still hand power to regional governments by statute, which is called **devolution**. The difference is that the central government may alter the statute, overriding what the devolved governments decide or widening their powers. In a federation the regional governments share powers with the central one as equal actors through a written constitution, and amending it needs the consent of both. That gives the regions a right to exist, and powers that the central government can't change on its own.
What, then, separates the two? The test is *who can change the division of powers*. Having an elected regional assembly, or a regional government with real work to do, doesn't settle it.

reveal.text: The extract names who can alter devolution, and that is the point to check whenever a regional government is called federal.

lead.text: Federations are easy to name. Wikipedia's list of examples today includes Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Germany, India, Switzerland and the United States. It's tempting to treat them as the usual case, so test that impression against a count.

reveal.text: Well-known examples show that federations exist, and a count shows how common they are.

lead.text: A federal constitution has to say who holds the powers nobody listed, and countries answer differently. Wikipedia reports that the German and American constitutions leave to the states every power not specifically granted to the federal government. Canada's and India's work the other way and leave to the federal government the powers not explicitly granted to the provinces or states. These leftover powers are called **residual powers**.

Australia lists its federal level's powers instead. Section 51 of its Constitution gives the Parliament of the Commonwealth power to make laws on a list of matters, among them defence, and currency, coinage and legal tender. The States keep all other areas of responsibility, and section 107 adds that a State parliament's powers continue as they were, unless the Constitution gives them exclusively to the Commonwealth or takes them away from the State.

The United States puts the idea in one sentence. In the Bill of Rights as it was proposed in 1789, the clause that became the Tenth Amendment says that powers the Constitution neither gives to the national government nor forbids the States to use stay with the States or the people.

reveal.text: The three countries whose constitutions list the federal powers leave the rest to the states, and Canada and India do the reverse.

lead.text: Whatever a federation does with unlisted powers, some powers go to the centre almost everywhere. Wikipedia says that in almost all federations the central government has foreign policy and national defence as exclusive federal powers, and Australia's section 51 shows the pattern, since defence and currency are on its list.

A division also needs a rule for when the two levels make conflicting laws. Australia's section 109 says that when a State law is inconsistent with a Commonwealth law, the Commonwealth law prevails and the State law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency. The sixth article of the United States Constitution has a similar rule: the Constitution, the laws made in pursuance of it and treaties are the supreme law of the land, binding judges in every State whatever a State's own constitution or laws say. So a level that keeps the unlisted powers still gives way where the other level acts within its powers.

James Madison saw a benefit in the division itself. In *The Federalist* No. 51, published in 1788, he describes the power the American people surrendered as divided first between two separate governments and then again among [[departments|The legislative, executive and judicial powers. Met in 'Montesquieu and the separation of powers'.]] in each. From that he draws a double security for the people's rights, since the governments will control each other while each is also controlled from within.

reveal.text: Section 109 settles the conflict by level and not by date, so a later State law gains nothing from being later.

lead.text: Since the division of powers is the point of a federation, the amending rule matters most. In the United States, Article 5 says that Congress proposes amendments when two thirds of both Houses think it necessary, or calls a convention to propose them on the application of two thirds of the States' legislatures. Either way, an amendment takes effect only when the legislatures of three fourths of the States, or conventions in three fourths of them, ratify it. Congress can propose, and it can't amend alone.

Australia's section 128 works differently. A proposed law must pass each House of the Parliament by an absolute majority, and between two and six months later it is put to the electors in each State. It goes forward only if it wins a majority of the votes cast in a majority of the States and also a majority of the votes cast across the whole country. In Australia that requirement is called a **double majority**, and Wikipedia says Switzerland's referendums to amend its constitution need the same two things, a majority overall and separate majorities in a majority of the cantons.

The double majority counts two different things. The national count asks how many *voters* said yes. The state count asks how many *states* did, and each state counts once, however many voters it has. A proposal has to win both counts.

steps.headline: In an invented federation of six states, a constitutional change gets 5,950,000 Yes votes and 5,620,000 No votes. Does it pass under a double majority?

lead.text: The states borrow Australia's names, but the country and every number are invented. The rule is the one in section 128: a majority of all the voters, and a majority of the voters in a majority of the states.

workedSteps.text: Start with the national count. Compare the two totals in the bottom row of the table.
Now the state count. In each state ask which side has more votes. Yes is ahead in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania, and behind in the other three.
A majority of six states is more than half of them, which is at least four, and Yes has carried three.
workedSteps.math: 3 of 6 states is not a majority

workedSteps.text: Yes wins the first count and loses the second, so the proposal doesn't pass, however large its national majority.

lead.text: Apply the test to a state described only by its rules, where nothing in the description uses the words federal or unitary.

reveal.text: The rule that matters is the amending rule. A constitution the centre can rewrite alone leaves the regions' powers in the centre's hands.

lessons.orientation: Say from a description or constitutional text whether a state is federal or unitary, which level holds a power, who can change the division, and whether a referendum passes under a double-majority rule.
lessons.nextAction: Apply Hobbes's argument to the relations between states, and judge whether a described Security Council vote passes.

blocks.text: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have a degree of power of their own, and so do the States of Australia, so at a glance the two arrangements look alike. In both, a region governs itself in some matters while a national government governs the whole country.

What separates them is a question about the arrangement itself. When the powers of the regions need to change, who can change them, and can the regions refuse? The answer sorts states into two families, and it shapes who keeps the powers nobody listed and how a constitution gets amended.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a state is federal or unitary, which level holds a power, and whether a referendum passes under a double-majority rule.
intro.whyItMatters: News about regions, states and provinces only makes sense once you know who can change what each level is allowed to do.

recap.keyIdea: A state is federal when its regional powers are fixed in a constitution that the centre can't change alone, and unitary when the centre can change them, so the question to ask is who can change the division.

blocks.text: In a unitary state the central government is supreme, and any power it delegates to regions, which is devolution, it can alter. In a federation the division is written in a constitution that both levels must agree to change, so the regions hold powers the centre can't take away by itself. Most UN members are unitary, though a significant share of the world's people and land is in federations.

Constitutions differ on who keeps the powers they don't list: the states in Germany, the United States and Australia, and the centre in Canada and India. In almost all federations the centre has foreign policy and defence, and where the two levels conflict, federal law prevails. Amending Australia's constitution takes a double majority, meaning a majority of all voters and majorities in a majority of the States, and the United States needs three fourths of the States.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson goes above the state and asks how states deal with one another when no government rules them all, using Hobbes's argument and the voting rule of the UN Security Council.

lessons.title: States among states

lead.text: In chapter 13 of *Leviathan*, published in 1651, Hobbes says that even if there had never been a time when individual people were at war with one another, kings and other persons of sovereign authority are always in a state of jealousy and in the posture of gladiators, because each of them is independent. Each keeps its weapons pointed at the others and its eyes on them: forts, garrisons and guns on the frontiers, and spies watching the neighbours. He calls that a posture of war, though he adds that because rulers use it to uphold the industry of their subjects, it doesn't bring the misery that comes with the liberty of individual men.

The textbook *International Relations*, from E-International Relations, gives the modern version. All states call themselves **sovereign**, which is a claim to govern their own territories exclusively and in their own fashion. Its latest count is no fewer than 195 states, and the United Nations has 193 members, so a few states stand outside it. With so many sovereigns and nothing above them, formal equality and sovereignty led, the textbook says, to the problem of **anarchy**.

Inside a country the word means that law and order have broken down. Between states it has a narrower meaning: a system in which power is decentralised and no shared institution has the right to enforce common rules. The word describes how the system is organised and says nothing in itself about how much fighting takes place.

reveal.text: Hobbes's gladiators are poised to fight without fighting, and anarchy in the textbook's sense describes institutions. Neither needs a battle.

lead.text: The textbook describes two schools of thought about this system. **Realists** link Hobbes to it. His people in the state of nature lived in a war of all against all, and since no contract of that kind exists between states, and nothing like a sovereign rules the world, disorder and fear prevail in international relations.

**Liberals** read the system differently. Immanuel Kant argued in the late eighteenth century that states sharing liberal values should have no reason to go to war with one another, and modern liberals have developed that idea into the democratic peace theory, which holds that democracies don't go to war with each other. The two schools also read international organisations differently. Realists believe states take part in them only when it serves their self-interest, and liberals argue that organisations are valuable because they help states reach decisions and put cooperation on a formal footing, which leads to peaceful outcomes.

afterFigure.text: The textbook presents both as theories, and the table sets them side by side, row by row. They differ in what they stress: the missing sovereign for the realists, and shared values and cooperation for the liberals.

lead.text: If nothing stands above states, is there any international law? The textbook pictures states as the principal actors, each holding supreme and exclusive authority over its own territory and following mainly customary and contractual rules in its dealings with others, with no world government above them. The International Court of Justice has a statute, and its Article 38 lists what the court may rely on when it decides cases: treaties, custom, general principles of law that most domestic legal systems share, such as acting in good faith, with judicial decisions and scholarly writings as a subsidiary means.

So a treaty is law for the states that made it even though no world government stands behind it. The rules between states come mainly from what states have agreed and from what they have long practised.

reveal.text: International law has its own sources, and a world government is not among the things it needs to be law.

lead.text: The United Nations is an **intergovernmental organisation**, a body of states whose power rests with the member governments and not with the organisation itself. Members can leave, the textbook adds, and in some cases they can ignore it. The UN has 193 member states, and its General Assembly is the most democratic organ, because each state has one vote whatever its size or wealth. Wikipedia notes that the blocking power of the Council's permanent members, described below, doesn't carry over into the General Assembly, whose votes are non-binding.

The Security Council is the most powerful organ. It has 15 members, five of them permanent (the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, France and China), and the General Assembly elects the other ten for two-year terms. Wikipedia says the five were the leading powers among the Second World War's Allies, or their recognised successors. Under Chapter VII of the Charter the Council can decide that peace and security are threatened and authorise responses, including the use of force, and its resolutions under that chapter, economic sanctions among them, bind all UN members.

lead.text: On a substantive matter, a decision of the Security Council needs the affirmative votes of nine of the fifteen members. A negative vote by a permanent member, called a **veto**, prevents adoption even if the draft has the nine votes, so a draft needs nine votes in favour *and* no permanent member against it. Through the end of 2024, Wikipedia counts approximately 120 vetoes cast by Russia and the Soviet Union, 89 by the United States, 29 by the United Kingdom and 16 each by France and China, so every one of the five has used the power.

Two exceptions matter. Procedural matters can't be vetoed, and the veto can't be used to stop an issue being discussed, though a procedural decision still needs nine votes. An abstention is not usually treated as a veto, so a permanent member that abstains lets a draft through, although an amendment to the Charter needs the active agreement of all five permanent members.
