steps.headline: A draft on a substantive matter gets eleven votes in favour, one vote against from a permanent member and three abstentions. Is it adopted?

lead.text: Take the two questions in turn, and keep the exceptions in mind.

workedSteps.text: First the votes in favour. The draft needs nine, and it has more than that.
Then the votes against. One of them comes from a permanent member, and a negative vote by a permanent member is a veto.
The three abstentions are not votes against, since an abstention isn't regarded as a veto in most cases, so they change nothing.
The draft has the votes but meets a veto, so it isn't adopted.

lead.text: Apply the rule to seven invented votes. Each can be adopted, blocked by a veto, or short of nine votes.

reveal.text: A draft can fail in two ways, by a veto or by too few votes, and the procedural vote and the abstentions were the cases where a permanent member's position did not stop it.

lead.text: A binding resolution is not the same as an enforced one. The United Nations has no military force of its own, though it can raise military and police personnel from contributions its members make, and the textbook says punitive measures are possible only when the Council's members are in accord and a group of states agrees to fund the operation and take part in it. The Council's decision comes first, and the states that carry it out come after.

The Charter also links the International Court of Justice to the Council. Article 94 has members undertake to comply with the court's decision in any case to which they are a party, and if one fails to, the other party may go to the Security Council, which may recommend or decide on measures. That is the Charter's own route for a party that doesn't comply, and it runs through a body in which five members hold a veto.

The Charter also rests the organisation on the sovereign equality of its members, and it bars the United Nations from intervening in matters that are essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction, though that doesn't stop enforcement measures under Chapter VII. Hobbes's remedy for the war of all against all was a sovereign with power over everyone, and the United Nations, as the Charter and the textbook describe it, is not that.

reveal.text: The Council decides, and whether anything happens next depends on states agreeing to act.

lead.text: Return to Hobbes with what you now know about the United Nations. His remedy for fear between people was a sovereign above them all, so ask whether the United Nations is one.

reveal.text: The United Nations' power comes from the states that belong to it, so it doesn't stand above them as Hobbes's sovereign stands above its subjects.

lessons.orientation: Apply Hobbes's argument to the relations between states, say what the Security Council can and cannot do, and judge whether a described resolution would pass.
lessons.nextAction: Choose a country and describe its regime, its executive, its courts and its levels of government, using the questions from this course.

blocks.text: Inside a country, a person who has been wronged can go to a court, and the state has the power to carry out what the court decides. Between countries there is no court that every state must accept and no police force that every state must obey. If one state breaks a promise to another, who is there to make it keep the promise?

Thomas Hobbes asked this kind of question about people who live with no common power over them, and he saw rulers in the same position. His answer bears on the one body that comes close to a shared authority over states, the UN Security Council, and on the rule it votes by.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply Hobbes's argument to states, say what the Security Council can and can't do, and judge whether a described draft resolution would pass.
intro.whyItMatters: News about sanctions, vetoes and the UN depends on a voting rule and on who is able to act, and both are easier to follow once you know them.

recap.keyIdea: Between states no shared authority enforces rules, and the Security Council, the nearest thing to one, acts only when nine members agree and no permanent member vetoes, and then only through states willing to carry it out.

blocks.text: Hobbes described rulers as gladiators with their weapons pointing at one another, and the textbook calls the resulting system anarchy: power is decentralised and no shared institution has the right to enforce common rules. Realists read that as disorder and fear, and liberals point to Kant and the democratic peace. International law still exists, with treaties, custom and general principles among its sources.

The United Nations is an intergovernmental organisation whose power rests with its member states. A Security Council draft on a substantive matter needs nine votes and no veto from a permanent member, an abstention is not usually a veto, and procedural matters and discussion can't be vetoed. Chapter VII resolutions are binding, but the UN has no army and needs states to act.

recap.nextHook: This is the last lesson of the course. You can use its questions on any country you read about: how its regime is classified, how its executive is chosen and removed, which level of government holds a power, and how it deals with other states.

questions.prompt: A governing coalition loses a vote of confidence and resigns, and a new government takes office the following week. What has happened to the state?
hints: Ask what a government is, on the account you have just read: a thing in itself, or an organisation acting for something else?
A state is a unit with sovereignty over a territory. Does a vote in the legislature change either of those?

acceptedIdeas: It carries on, because the government only acted for it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It carries on, because the government only acted for it

questions.onCorrect: Elections, resignations and coups change who staffs the government. The state they act for is the same one afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the two as one thing. A government is an organisation of people acting on the state's behalf, so a change of government leaves the state, with its territory and sovereignty, where it was.
Sovereignty belongs to the state over its territory. The people who exercise it for the state can change without the state losing it.

choices.label: It ends, because a state is whatever its government is
It carries on, because the government only acted for it
It ends, because a state cannot keep its sovereignty without the government that exercised it

questions.prompt: A legislature votes to take the farms of everyone in one province and give them to its own members. According to Locke, what follows?
hints: Think back to what Locke says people hand over when they consent, and what it is handed over for.
The case describes a legislature acting against the property of the people it governs. What would that do to the trust?

acceptedIdeas: It has broken its trust, and the people no longer owe it obedience
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has broken its trust, and the people no longer owe it obedience

questions.onCorrect: In Locke's account such legislators place themselves at war with the people, who are then released from further obedience.

misconceptions.feedback: Locke gives a majority no such power. The legislature holds its power on trust for the people's security and property, so a vote does not make an attack on them lawful.
Locke's test is met when legislators endeavour to take away the people's property. The attempt is the breach, so the people need not wait for the loss.

choices.label: It has broken its trust, and the people no longer owe it obedience
The act is lawful, because the legislature's majority voted for it under its own rules
The people must obey until the farms have actually been taken

questions.prompt: Here are two extracts, one from Hobbes and one from Locke. What do both writers say a state supplies?

extracts.text: And Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.
extracts.who: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651)
extracts.when: written during the English Civil War and published in 1651
extracts.kind: A work of political theory arguing for an absolute sovereign

extracts.text: there often wants power to back and support the sentence when right, and to give it due execution
extracts.who: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
extracts.when: published anonymously in 1689, probably drafted about 1680
extracts.kind: A work of political philosophy setting out a society based on natural rights and contract theory

hints: Look at what Hobbes says a covenant lacks, and what Locke says a sentence lacks.
Both writers name the same missing thing in two different settings. What is it?

acceptedIdeas: Power able to enforce what has been agreed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power able to enforce what has been agreed

questions.onCorrect: Hobbes and Locke differ on what gives anyone the right to rule, yet each finds that agreements and sentences need force behind them.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither extract says anything about how a ruler is chosen. Both are about what stands behind an agreement or a sentence.
Neither extract mentions who makes the laws. Each is about the force needed to give a promise or a sentence effect.

choices.label: Power able to enforce what has been agreed
A ruler chosen by those who are governed
Laws made by the people's own representatives

questions.prompt: Each of these is an invented claim to rule. Which of Weber's three bases does each one rest on?
hints: Ask where the authority is said to come from: the past, a person, or a procedure.
Two of the claims fall under each type, and a claim that ends when one person goes is a clue.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The king's six hundred years and the village council are traditional, the courageous leader and the founder are charismatic, and the written tax code and the statutes are rational-legal.

questions.onCorrect: Weber's three types ask what the ruled believe supports the rule: custom, a person or a procedure.

items.label: We obey the king because his family has ruled here for six hundred years
items.explanation: The claim rests on a long history of rule, which is custom and habit.

items.label: Citizens follow her because they trust her courage and gifts more than any office she holds
items.explanation: The authority comes from the leader's personal qualities, whatever office she holds.

items.label: Tax officials act under a written code, and citizens believe the code was made by lawful procedure
items.explanation: Obedience rests on institutional procedure and on belief that the procedure was followed.

items.label: The village accepts the council's rulings because that is how disputes have always been settled
items.explanation: Acceptance rests on the way things have always been done.

items.label: Crowds obey the movement's founder, and the movement fades when he dies
items.explanation: A movement that depends on one person and disappears without him fits the charismatic type.

items.label: Courts and ministries follow statutes, and an order not made under a statute is not obeyed
items.explanation: Authority is tied to law and procedure, so an order outside the procedure has no force.

questions.prompt: A government has held office for decades and most of its citizens say they dislike it. Which statement about its survival fits the accounts of legitimacy you have read?
hints: Weber says legitimacy is about whether subjects regard the claim to rule as valid. Which subjects?
Is popularity with the whole population the only thing that could keep a regime in place?

acceptedIdeas: A small, influential elite can regard it as legitimate and so keep it in place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A small, influential elite can regard it as legitimate and so keep it in place

questions.onCorrect: An unpopular regime can last while those whose belief matters most still treat its rule as valid.

misconceptions.feedback: Weber held that democracy is unnecessary for legitimacy, and the article on legitimacy says unpopular regimes can survive on an influential elite's belief in them.
On Weber's account a state is legitimate when its subjects see its claim to rule as valid, and a small elite counts among those subjects. Dahl's reservoir also makes legitimacy part of stability.

choices.label: It cannot be legitimate, because legitimacy always requires the support of most citizens
It survives by force alone, so legitimacy plays no part in its survival
A small, influential elite can regard it as legitimate and so keep it in place

questions.prompt: Two years after a war, rival commanders still control the roads around a country's capital. Each charges a toll and punishes anyone who refuses to pay, and the national police no longer go there. In Weber's definition of a state, what has the national government lost on those roads?
hints: Weber's definition names one thing a state's government keeps in its territory. Which?
The commanders are doing something only a state is supposed to do. What is it?

acceptedIdeas: monopoly of the legitimate use of force
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: monopoly of the legitimate use of force
acceptedAlternatives: monopoly on the legitimate use of force
monopoly of the legitimate use of violence

questions.onCorrect: The government no longer holds the monopoly of the legitimate use of force on those roads, so on Weber's definition it is not acting as the state there.

misconceptions.feedback: Sovereignty over a territory belongs to the state, and losing the monopoly of force is how that sovereignty fails in practice. The question asks for the feature Weber's definition names.
Legitimacy is part of the definition, but it qualifies what the state keeps. Name the thing it keeps, and say whose use of it counts.

questions.prompt: A ruler redraws the electoral districts and rewrites the list of voters, without the people's consent, so that only his supporters can be elected. Using Locke's reasoning in the extract, what follows?

extracts.text: When, by the arbitrary power of the prince, the electors, or ways of election, are altered, without the consent, and contrary to the common interest of the people, there also the legislative is altered: for, if others than those whom the society hath authorized thereunto, do chuse, or in another way than what the society hath prescribed, those chosen are not the legislative appointed by the people.
extracts.who: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
extracts.when: published anonymously in 1689, probably drafted about 1680
extracts.kind: A work of political philosophy setting out a society based on natural rights and contract theory

hints: Look for who has authorised the people who are chosen, and by what way they are chosen.
Locke counts the change of electors as a change to the legislature itself. What does he say those chosen are not?

acceptedIdeas: Those chosen are not the legislature the people appointed, so it has been altered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Those chosen are not the legislature the people appointed, so it has been altered

questions.onCorrect: Locke's test covers a quiet breach of trust through the ways of election as well as an open attack on property.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract treats a change made by the ruler's arbitrary power, without consent and against the common interest, as an alteration of the legislature, so the ruler's power to set the rules does not make the change lawful.
The extract says the legislature is altered when the ways of election are, and does not wait for a harmful law to follow.

choices.label: The change is lawful, because the ruler holds the power to set the rules of election
Those chosen are not the legislature the people appointed, so it has been altered
Nothing follows until the new legislature passes a law that harms the people

questions.prompt: A government holds elections and passes laws, but it cannot protect its citizens from violence. In Mittiga's two parts, which kind of legitimacy is in doubt first?
hints: Which of the two parts is about safety and security?
Mittiga says what follows when a government cannot fulfil the basic security functions. Does he say anything like that about elections?

acceptedIdeas: Foundational legitimacy, because it covers the ability to keep citizens safe
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Foundational legitimacy, because it covers the ability to keep citizens safe

questions.onCorrect: A government that fails the security question has no basis for the second question, however many laws it passes.

misconceptions.feedback: Contingent legitimacy concerns whether power is exercised in acceptable ways, and holding elections does not settle that. The failure here is in the first part.
The article on legitimacy says elections do not automatically grant it, and Mittiga says a government that cannot meet the basic security functions is not legitimate at all.

choices.label: Foundational legitimacy, because it covers the ability to keep citizens safe
Contingent legitimacy, because it covers whether elections are held
Neither, because holding elections is enough to make a government legitimate

questions.prompt: In a city the rich are in the majority, and they hold every office and rule in their own interest. Which name does Aristotle's refinement give this government?
hints: Ask Aristotle's two questions in turn: how many rule, and whose good do they serve?
His refinement says the number does not decide between oligarchy and democracy. What does?

acceptedIdeas: Oligarchy, since the rich rule however many they are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Oligarchy, since the rich rule however many they are

questions.onCorrect: On Aristotle's refinement the rich ruling for themselves is an oligarchy, whatever share of the city they make up.

misconceptions.feedback: Aristotle separates oligarchy from democracy by wealth, whatever the number of rulers. Rule by the rich is an oligarchy even when the rich are a majority.
An aristocracy is rule by a few for the common good. These rulers look only to their own interest, so the form is a corrupt one.

choices.label: Oligarchy, since the rich rule however many they are
Democracy, since a majority of the citizens hold the offices
Aristocracy, since those who rule are the best off

questions.prompt: A report says that a country holds regular multi-party elections for president and legislature, and concludes that it is a democracy. Which question would you ask before accepting that?
hints: Authoritarian states can hold elections that are managed. What would make an election more than a managed one?
Think about what voters and parties must be free to do for a vote to mean something.

acceptedIdeas: Whether citizens have the freedoms that make elections meaningful
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether citizens have the freedoms that make elections meaningful

questions.onCorrect: Freedoms such as association and expression are what separate elections that mean something from those that only look like them.

misconceptions.feedback: The title of the head of government is a question about the type of system. It says nothing about whether the elections mean anything.
Regular elections are what the report already describes, and authoritarian regimes can hold them regularly too. Regularity does not show that they are meaningful.

choices.label: Whether the country has a president or a prime minister
Whether citizens have the freedoms that make elections meaningful
Whether the elections have been held regularly for many years running

questions.prompt: Each of these six descriptions is invented. Which of the four categories fits each one?
hints: Start with the first question: is there a multi-party election for the executive and the legislature at all?
For the descriptions with elections, ask whether the freedoms that make them meaningful are present, and then whether the executive is limited.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ruling family and the single-party slate are closed autocracies, the banned meetings and the controlled broadcasters are electoral autocracies, the unchecked president is an electoral democracy, and the free elections with courts and equal rights are a liberal democracy.

questions.onCorrect: The three questions separate all four categories, and the descriptions differ in the point at which they fail.

items.label: The ruling family appoints every minister, and no national office is filled by a multi-party election
items.explanation: Citizens cannot choose the chief executive or the legislature in multi-party elections.

items.label: Multi-party elections are held for president and legislature, but opposition meetings are banned and its newspapers are closed during each campaign
items.explanation: Elections are held, but the freedoms of association and expression that make them meaningful are missing.

items.label: Parties compete on equal terms in free and fair elections, and the elected president is not checked by the courts or the legislature
items.explanation: The elections are meaningful, free and fair, but the executive is not constrained as a liberal democracy requires.

items.label: Free elections choose the president and legislature, courts overturn unlawful orders, the legislature questions ministers, and minorities have equal rights before the law
items.explanation: Free elections are joined by individual and minority rights and by constraints on the executive.

items.label: Voters choose among parties, but the ruling party owns the main broadcasters and the electoral officers are its members
items.explanation: Multi-party elections exist, and the control of broadcasting and of the officials who run them means they are not free and fair.

items.label: A single party presents the only list of candidates, and voters may only approve or reject it
items.explanation: There is no multi-party election through which citizens choose the executive or the legislature.

questions.prompt: A report describes a country where elections are held regularly and the opposition wins seats, but the ruling party controls the main broadcasters, the courts rarely rule against it and opposition rallies are sometimes banned. A reader says it fits none of the four boxes and so the description is useless. What is the best reply?
hints: Which features in the description are democratic and which are autocratic?
A scale from democratic to authoritarian leaves room for a description that has some of each.

acceptedIdeas: Its mix of features places it between the poles and shows what is missing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its mix of features places it between the poles and shows what is missing

questions.onCorrect: A hybrid description is informative because the pattern of present and missing features is what it reports.

misconceptions.feedback: Elections that the ruling party can tilt do not settle the matter. The definitions ask whether the freedoms that make elections meaningful are present.
The country also holds regular elections that the opposition can win seats in, which are democratic features. A mixed description is a hybrid, and calling it one pole leaves out half of it.

choices.label: Its mix of features places it between the poles and shows what is missing
It is a democracy, because elections are held and the opposition wins seats
It is an autocracy, because the ruling party controls the broadcasters and courts

questions.prompt: A student reads this passage and concludes that Aristotle was against rule by the many. What is wrong with that conclusion?

extracts.text: a kingdom may degenerate into a tyranny, an aristocracy into an oligarchy, and a state into a democracy. Now a tyranny is a monarchy where the good of one man only is the object of government, an oligarchy considers only the rich, and a democracy only the poor; but neither of them have a common good in view.
extracts.who: Aristotle, Politics, Book III (Jowett translation, 1885)
extracts.when: written in the 4th century BC
extracts.kind: A work of political philosophy

hints: Look at which form the passage says a state degenerates into, and what that form considers.
Aristotle's two questions are how many rule and whose good they serve. Which of them does the student leave out?

acceptedIdeas: He names only the corrupt form democracy, and rule by the many for the common good is good
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: He names only the corrupt form democracy, and rule by the many for the common good is good

questions.onCorrect: Aristotle judges a form by whose good it serves as well as by how many rule.

misconceptions.feedback: Aristotle's scheme has a good form of rule by the many, which Jowett calls a state. What he condemns is rule by the poor for the poor alone.
In the passage democracy is a corruption of a state, so it is a wrong form, far from the best. The modern use of the word is a different one.

choices.label: He opposed rule by the many, since he thought the many could never look to the common good
He used the word as it is used today, and thought it the best form of government
He names only the corrupt form democracy, and rule by the many for the common good is good

questions.prompt: In one country elections are free and fair and parties compete on equal terms, but the courts and the legislature do not restrain the executive and minorities have no special protection. What term does the lesson give to a democracy of this kind?
hints: The country passes the tests for meaningful elections but lacks the limits that make a democracy liberal.
The lesson gives two terms for a democracy that has the elections and lacks the rule of law and checks on the executive.

acceptedIdeas: illiberal democracy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: illiberal democracy

questions.onCorrect: Such a democracy holds the elections and lacks the limits on the majority, which is why it is called illiberal, or procedural, and in the regime data it is an electoral democracy.

misconceptions.feedback: A liberal democracy has the limits this country lacks: minority rights, equality before the law and constraints on the executive.
In this country the elections are free and fair, and an electoral autocracy lacks the freedoms that make them so.

questions.prompt: A country's president and legislature are chosen in multi-party elections. Observers find that opposition candidates are regularly barred from the ballot and campaign meetings are banned, though the votes themselves are counted accurately. Which category fits best?
hints: Answer the first question first: can citizens choose the executive and legislature in multi-party elections?
Then ask whether freedoms such as association and expression are present.

acceptedIdeas: Electoral autocracy, since the elections lack the freedoms that make them meaningful
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Electoral autocracy, since the elections lack the freedoms that make them meaningful

questions.onCorrect: Accurate counting is not enough, because the freedoms around the vote decide whether the election is meaningful.

misconceptions.feedback: An electoral democracy needs elections that are meaningful, free and fair, and barring candidates and banning meetings removes the freedoms that make them so.
In a closed autocracy citizens cannot choose the executive or legislature through multi-party elections at all. Here they can, though the freedoms that make the elections meaningful are missing.

choices.label: Electoral democracy, since the votes are counted accurately in multi-party elections
Electoral autocracy, since the elections lack the freedoms that make them meaningful
Closed autocracy, since the government restricts how the opposition can campaign

questions.prompt: Each of these five countries has a run of years coded as a liberal democracy. In what order does each first appear as one, earliest first?
hints: Look for the first stretch of liberal democracy in each bar, and ignore earlier years coded in other categories.
Three of the five were electoral democracies at some point before they were first coded as liberal democracies, and one has a gap in its bar.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sweden is coded as a liberal democracy from 1922, France from 1947, Japan from 1952, the United States from 1969 and Germany from 1991.

questions.onCorrect: A country's earlier runs in other categories do not count, since the question is about when it first meets the definition of a liberal democracy.

questions.prompt: In this regime file the other countries' series begin in 1789, but South Africa's first row is 1900. What can a reader say about South Africa before 1900?
hints: Ask what the file says about the years before 1900, and whether it says anything at all.
An empty row can arise for several reasons. Does the file tell you which?

acceptedIdeas: Only that the file has no rows for those years, and it gives no reason

The word is used in the clauses on how a President, a Vice President and civil officers are removed.

acceptedIdeas: impeachment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: impeachment

questions.onCorrect: The process is impeachment: the House has the sole power to impeach, the Senate to try, and a conviction needs two thirds of the members present.

misconceptions.feedback: A veto is the President's return of a bill. The process in the question is a way of removing an officer.

questions.prompt: A bill to spend public money on new roads is introduced in the Australian Senate. What does the 1900 text say about that?

extracts.text: Proposed laws appropriating revenue or moneys, or imposing taxation, shall not originate in the Senate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It bars the bill, since proposed laws appropriating revenue may not begin in the Senate

questions.onCorrect: The text sets a limit on where a money bill may begin, and the limit falls on the Senate.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says laws appropriating revenue or imposing taxation may not begin in the Senate. The Senate cannot start such a bill.
The extract names the Senate as the body that may not originate such laws. It gives no such power to the Governor-General.

choices.label: It bars the bill, since proposed laws appropriating revenue may not begin in the Senate
It allows the bill, since the Senate may propose any law that the House of Representatives can
It bars the bill, since only the Governor-General may propose laws about spending money

questions.prompt: In country A the legislature can vote the head of government out of office. In country B the head of government is elected by the voters for a fixed term, and the legislature cannot remove them except in extraordinary cases. In both countries most of the legislature has now turned against the head of government. Whose position is more likely to end within the week?
hints: Ask who has the power to end each head of government's time in office.
In country B, what does a majority of the legislature turning against the head of government actually allow the legislature to do?

acceptedIdeas: Country A's head of government, since the legislature there can remove them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Country A's head of government, since the legislature there can remove them

choices.label: Country A's head of government, since the legislature there can remove them
Country B's head of government, since voters can end the term of anyone they elect
Neither one, since a head of government holds the same powers in every country

questions.onCorrect: A legislature that can vote out the head of government can act on its opposition at once, which is why the answer to 'who can remove them?' matters so much.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the description lets voters end the term early. In country B the voters chose a head of government for a fixed term, and losing the legislature's support does not end it.
The powers can be alike while the way of removing them differs. What the description changes between A and B is who can end the term, and that decides whose position is at risk.

questions.prompt: The extract describes how Germany's head of government is chosen. Which kind of system does that procedure fit?

extracts.text: Germany where under the German Basic Law (constitution) the Bundestag votes on a candidate nominated by the federal president.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Parliamentary system" (revision 1384859356, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Who has the last word on whether a candidate becomes head of government?
Compare the head of government's dependence on parliament here with the definition of confidence you have just read.

acceptedIdeas: Parliamentary, since the head of government depends on a vote of parliament
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Parliamentary, since the head of government depends on a vote of parliament

choices.label: Presidential, since a president takes part by nominating the candidate
Parliamentary, since the head of government depends on a vote of parliament
Semi-presidential, since both a president and a legislature are involved

questions.onCorrect: The president names a candidate but the Bundestag decides, so the head of government depends on parliament, which is the mark of a parliamentary system.

misconceptions.feedback: Nominating a candidate does not make a system presidential. In a presidential system citizens elect the head of government and the legislature cannot dismiss them, whereas here the Bundestag has the deciding vote.
A semi-presidential system has an executive president who is independent of the legislature. The extract gives the president only the part of nominating a candidate, and the Bundestag's vote decides.

questions.prompt: A country's leader is called president, is chosen by a party congress, and cannot be removed by any vote of an assembly. What does the article on presidential systems warn about a case like this?

extracts.text: However, dictators or leaders of one-party states, whether popularly elected or not, often carry the title of president.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Presidential system" (revision 1384698936, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Does the extract say anything about how the leader is chosen or removed, or only about what the leader is called?
Which two questions did the lesson say to ask about any head of government?

acceptedIdeas: That the title president does not make a system presidential
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the title president does not make a system presidential

choices.label: That a leader chosen by a congress is really a prime minister
That every one-party state is a semi-presidential system
That the title president does not make a system presidential

questions.onCorrect: A title tells you what someone is called. The two questions, how they are chosen and who can remove them, tell you which system it is.

misconceptions.feedback: Being chosen by a congress does not turn a president into a prime minister. The article's warning is about titles: they do not settle which system a country has.

The article says only that leaders of one-party states often carry the title of president. A system is semi-presidential when a prime minister and cabinet answer to a legislature, and nothing here says that.

questions.prompt: In country K a president elected by the voters names a prime minister and cabinet. Parliament can force the cabinet out by a vote of no confidence, and the president can dismiss it as well. Why does the first of those two powers rule out calling K a presidential system?
hints: Think about what the definition of a presidential system says about the legislature and dismissal.
Which of the three families lets a legislature remove a cabinet by a vote of no confidence?

acceptedIdeas: In a presidential system the assembly cannot normally dismiss the executive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In a presidential system the assembly cannot normally dismiss the executive

choices.label: In a presidential system the assembly cannot normally dismiss the executive
A president who names the cabinet is always a sign of a parliamentary system
Parliamentary systems are the only ones with a prime minister

questions.onCorrect: Because parliament can force the cabinet out, the cabinet answers to the legislature, which a presidential system does not allow.

misconceptions.feedback: A president can name a cabinet in several systems, including semi-presidential ones. What decides the matter here is who can remove the cabinet.
Semi-presidential systems also have a prime minister. The prime minister's accountability to the legislature is the point, and not the title.

questions.prompt: Source A is a remark of Montesquieu's and Source B is a rule of Australia's constitution. What does Source A say about the arrangement in Source B?

extracts.text: But if there were no monarch, and the executive power should be committed to a certain number of persons selected from the legislative body, there would be an end then of liberty; by reason the two powers would be united, as the same persons would sometimes possess, and would be always able to possess, a share in both.
extracts.who: Montesquieu, The Spirit of Laws, Book XI, chapter 6 (Nugent translation, 1750)
extracts.when: published in 1748, in the English translation of 1750
extracts.kind: A treatise on political theory

extracts.text: After the first general election no Minister of State shall hold office for a longer period than three months unless he is or becomes a senator or a member of the House of Representatives.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 64
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

hints: Who exercises executive power under the rule in Source B, and where else do they sit?
Which power does Source A say would be united with the executive if the same persons held both?

acceptedIdeas: It unites the two powers in the same persons, which he thought would end liberty
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It unites the two powers in the same persons, which he thought would end liberty

choices.label: It follows his advice, since he wanted executive officers drawn from the legislature
It unites the two powers in the same persons, which he thought would end liberty
It has no bearing, since his remark concerned the judges

questions.onCorrect: Australia's rule puts ministers in the legislature, which is the union Montesquieu warned against. The next screen gives a writer who praised that union.

misconceptions.feedback: In the passage he says the reverse: persons selected from the legislative body to hold executive power would unite the two powers, and he saw that as the end of liberty.
The remark is about the executive power, and about who may exercise it. Montesquieu's views on judges come elsewhere in the chapter.

questions.prompt: Here are six invented descriptions of how an executive is chosen and removed. Which family does each one fit?
hints: Ask of each description who can remove the head of government or the cabinet.
Look for a president and a prime minister in the same description, which points to the semi-presidential family.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Parliamentary: the leader who needs the assembly's majority and the prime minister who sits in the lower house. Presidential: the head of government elected for a fixed term and the president who picks a cabinet the assembly cannot remove. Semi-presidential: the elected president with a prime minister whose cabinet the assembly can force out, and the president and prime minister who share executive power.

questions.onCorrect: Each description is placed by the same two questions: how the head of government is chosen and who can remove them.

items.label: The head of government is the leader whose party can win a majority vote in the assembly, and must resign if the assembly passes a no-confidence motion
items.explanation: The head of government depends on a majority of the assembly, which can end the term by withdrawing confidence.

items.label: The head of government is elected by the voters for a fixed four-year term, and the assembly cannot dismiss them except for a crime
items.explanation: Citizens elect the head of government, and the assembly can remove them only in an extraordinary case such as a crime.

items.label: A directly elected president appoints a prime minister, and the assembly can force the prime minister's cabinet to resign by a no-confidence vote
items.explanation: A president and a prime minister both exist, and the cabinet answers to the legislature.

items.label: A monarch appoints as prime minister the person with most support in the lower house, and the prime minister sits in that house
items.explanation: Support in the lower house decides who leads, so the head of government depends on the legislature whoever names them.

items.label: Voters elect the president and the assembly separately, the president picks the cabinet, and the assembly has no power to remove it
items.explanation: The head of government is elected apart from the assembly, which cannot dismiss the cabinet.

items.label: A president and a prime minister both hold executive power, and the prime minister answers to both the president and the assembly
items.explanation: The prime minister is dually accountable, which marks the president-parliamentary kind of semi-presidential system.

questions.prompt: These two extracts come from articles on presidential and semi-presidential systems. What do the two arguments have in common?

extracts.text: James Wilson, who advocated for a presidential system at the constitutional convention, maintained that a single chief executive would provide for greater public accountability than a group and thereby protect against tyranny by making it plain who was responsible for executive actions.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Presidential system" (revision 1384698936, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

extracts.text: It creates a sense of confusion towards accountability, as there is no relatively clear sense of who is responsible for policy successes and failures.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Semi-presidential system" (revision 1383704652, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Underline in each extract what is said about responsibility.
One extract praises an arrangement and the other criticises one: what value do both appeal to?

acceptedIdeas: Both treat clarity about who is responsible as what voters need
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both treat clarity about who is responsible as what voters need

choices.label: Both argue that the legislature should choose the executive
Both treat clarity about who is responsible as what voters need
Both favour giving the president a fixed term

questions.onCorrect: Wilson and the critic of semi-presidentialism reach opposite verdicts from one shared test, which is whether it is plain who is responsible.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither passage mentions who chooses the executive. Wilson argues for a single executive, and the second extract criticises a system where responsibility is unclear.
Fixed terms are not mentioned in either extract. They are about whether people can tell who is responsible for what the executive does.

questions.prompt: Country Q has a president with executive power and a prime minister who answers to parliament. Voters elect a president from one party, and then a parliament in which a rival party is strongest, which backs a prime minister from that rival party. What is such a situation called?
hints: The term came from France in the 1980s.
It describes a president and a prime minister who come from different parties and still have to share the executive.

acceptedIdeas: cohabitation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: cohabitation

questions.onCorrect: A president and a prime minister from different parties are in cohabitation, which can work as a system of checks or as a standoff.

misconceptions.feedback: A coalition is a government of several parties working together. Here the two parties are on opposite sides, one holding the presidency and the other holding the prime minister's office.

Gridlock describes a stalemate, which can happen but does not have to. This question asks for the name of the arrangement itself: a president and a prime minister from rival parties who share the executive.

questions.prompt: Country R has an executive president who is independent of the legislature. The president names a prime minister, but only parliament may approve the choice, and only parliament can remove the prime minister, by a vote of no confidence. Which kind of system is this?
hints: Does the legislature hold any power over the prime minister in country R?
Of the two kinds of semi-presidential system, which one lets the president dismiss the prime minister as well?

acceptedIdeas: Semi-presidential, of the premier-presidential kind
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Semi-presidential, of the premier-presidential kind

choices.label: Semi-presidential, of the president-parliamentary kind
Presidential, since the president names the prime minister
Semi-presidential, of the premier-presidential kind

questions.onCorrect: Parliament alone can remove the prime minister, which is the premier-presidential kind and sits close to a parliamentary system.

misconceptions.feedback: In the president-parliamentary kind the president can also dismiss the prime minister and cabinet. In R only parliament can remove them.
In a presidential system the cabinet does not answer to the legislature by a vote of no confidence. In R it does, so the system is semi-presidential.

questions.prompt: A court rules that a minister's order is unlawful, and the minister simply ignores the ruling. Whose help does the court need, in the end, to make its ruling count for anything?
hints: Think about what a court has to hand: judges and a written ruling. What does it lack that a government has?
The minister belongs to one branch and the court to another. Which branch would have to act for the ruling to be carried out?

acceptedIdeas: The executive, since carrying out a ruling needs the means that branch holds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The executive, since carrying out a ruling needs the means that branch holds

choices.label: Its own officers, since a court keeps the means to enforce what it decides
The executive, since carrying out a ruling needs the means that branch holds
The legislature, since only a new statute can give a ruling any real force

questions.onCorrect: A court can decide but it cannot carry out its decisions, which is why Hamilton says it depends on the executive arm even for the effect of its judgments.

misconceptions.feedback: Hamilton says the judiciary has no influence over the sword or the purse, so it has no strength of its own to enforce a ruling. A court can decide a case, and someone else has to make the decision stick.
A new statute would still need someone to carry it out. The aid that Hamilton says a court depends on comes from the executive arm.

questions.prompt: Source A describes judges who only pronounce the words of the law. What further duty does Source B give to courts?

extracts.text: the national judges are no more than the mouth that pronounces the words of the law, mere passive beings, incapable of moderating either its force or rigor.
extracts.who: Montesquieu, The Spirit of Laws, Book XI, chapter 6 (Nugent translation, 1750)
extracts.when: published in 1748, in the English translation of 1750
extracts.kind: A treatise on political theory

extracts.text: Limitations of this kind can be preserved in practice no other way than through the medium of courts of justice, whose duty it must be to declare all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void.
extracts.who: Alexander Hamilton, The Federalist No. 78
extracts.when: published under the name Publius in McLean's edition on 28 May 1788
extracts.kind: An essay written to persuade voters to ratify the Constitution of the United States

hints: Compare what each judge does with a law that already exists: apply it as written, or test it against something above it.
In Source B, what happens to an act that conflicts with the Constitution, and who is given the duty to make it happen?

acceptedIdeas: To declare void an act that goes against the Constitution
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To declare void an act that goes against the Constitution

choices.label: To soften a statute whose force or rigour seems too great
To draft the statutes that the legislature then votes on
To declare void an act that goes against the Constitution

questions.onCorrect: Montesquieu's judge speaks the law as it stands. Hamilton's judge also tests an act against the Constitution and declares it void if it conflicts.

misconceptions.feedback: Source A rules that out: its judges are incapable of moderating the law's force or rigour. What Source B adds is a test of an act against the Constitution, which is a different task from softening a law.
Neither source gives judges a part in writing statutes. Source B concerns acts that contradict the Constitution, and the duty it names belongs to the courts that judge them.

questions.prompt: A critic says that an elected legislature speaks for the people, so unelected judges who set aside its statute put themselves above the people's representatives. Which link in Hamilton's chain answers the critic most directly?
hints: The critic's complaint is about rank: who stands above whom. Which link says something about rank?
Look for the link that names a power higher than the legislature and higher than the courts as well.

acceptedIdeas: The people's power stands above both the courts and the legislature
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The people's power stands above both the courts and the legislature

choices.label: Courts have neither force nor will, and only judgment is left to them
The people's power stands above both the courts and the legislature
Limits on a legislature last only if courts can void breaches

questions.onCorrect: Hamilton says review sets no court above the legislature, because the people's power stands above both.

misconceptions.feedback: That link answers a different worry, that judges will put their own preferences in place of the law. It says nothing about whose authority ranks higher.
That link says why courts are needed if a limit is to mean anything. It leaves the critic's point about who ranks above whom unanswered.

questions.prompt: Each of these six invented countries lets its courts do something different about a statute that seems to break the constitution. Which of the three approaches does each one follow?
hints: Ask first whether any court at all may rule on a statute. Then ask whether the power belongs to many courts or to one.
A court that hears everyday cases as well as reviewing statutes belongs in the middle group.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A and D allow no review of statutes. B and F leave review to general courts. C and E give it to a constitutional court, which in E the ordinary courts can only prompt.

questions.onCorrect: Each approach turns on who may rule on a statute: no court, any ordinary court, or one specialised court that other courts can only prompt.

items.label: Country A's constitution tells judges to apply every statute as written and forbids any court to rule on whether one is constitutional
items.explanation: No court may rule on a statute, which is the first approach, as in the Netherlands.

items.label: In Country B any court hearing a case may rule that a statute conflicts with the constitution
items.explanation: The ordinary courts do the reviewing themselves, as in Australia, Canada and the United States.

items.label: Country C has one court whose only work is to decide whether statutes conform to the constitution
items.explanation: A court that does this and nothing else is a constitutional court, as in Germany.

items.label: In Country D judges say openly that they cannot strike down a statute, because the legislature is supreme
items.explanation: A strong attachment to legislative supremacy is the reason given for the first approach in the United Kingdom.

items.label: In Country E ordinary courts may ask the constitutional court to look at a statute but may not decide the question themselves
items.explanation: Other courts may start the process but only the constitutional court decides, as in the Austrian system.

items.label: In Country F the supreme court and the regional high courts, which also hear everyday cases, can invalidate statutes that go against the constitution
items.explanation: Courts that also hear ordinary cases and can review statutes follow the second approach, as in India.

questions.prompt: A United Kingdom court hears a case and finds that an Act of Parliament conflicts with the Convention rights brought into British law by the Human Rights Act 1998. What can the court do about the Act?
hints: Recall what the lesson said about British judges and the power to strike down primary legislation.
The Human Rights Act gave courts a particular power. Does it end the Act's force, or ask someone else to act?

acceptedIdeas: Issue a declaration of incompatibility, asking Parliament to put the breach right
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Issue a declaration of incompatibility, asking Parliament to put the breach right

choices.label: Issue a declaration of incompatibility, asking Parliament to put the breach right
Strike the Act down, ending its force from the date of the ruling in the case
Decline to comment, since British courts may not examine an Act of Parliament at all

questions.onCorrect: A declaration of incompatibility tells Parliament that the Act breaches the Convention, and Parliament decides what to do about it.

misconceptions.feedback: British judges cannot strike down an Act of Parliament, because of a strong attachment to legislative supremacy. The Act stays in force until Parliament changes it.
The Human Rights Act gave courts the power to examine an Act against the Convention and to say so in a declaration. What they lack is the power to disapply the Act.

questions.prompt: An official refuses a residence permit and the applicant asks a court to review the refusal. Which question does the court usually ask?
hints: Remember what separates a review from an appeal: does the court retake the decision, or check how it was made?
Which of these questions could be answered without the judge deciding the permit afresh?

acceptedIdeas: Was the refusal made in line with the law and with fair procedure?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Was the refusal made in line with the law and with fair procedure?

choices.label: Does the applicant's need for the permit outweigh the state's reasons?
Would the court itself have refused the permit on the same facts?
Was the refusal made in line with the law and with fair procedure?

questions.onCorrect: Review checks the decision against the law and fair procedure, and the court does not usually take the decision over.

misconceptions.feedback: Weighing need against the state's reasons is deciding the application afresh. A review asks whether the official followed the law and fair procedure when deciding.
That would be the court taking the decision itself. In a review the court does not usually take the decision over, so its own view of the permit is not the test.

questions.prompt: Two invented news items arrive on the same day. In one country 'the Constitutional Court struck down the pensions law'. In another, 'a court declared the pensions law incompatible with the Human Rights Act'. What does the difference tell you about the two countries?
hints: A court that strikes a law down ends its force. What does a declaration of incompatibility leave in place?
Which country's report says what happens to the statute next, and which one only says what the court found?

acceptedIdeas: In the first a court can end a statute's force, in the second Parliament decides what happens to the Act
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the first a court can end a statute's force, in the second Parliament decides what happens to the Act

choices.label: Both countries let courts strike statutes down, and the second report just describes a lower court's ruling
In the first a court can end a statute's force, in the second Parliament decides what happens to the Act
The second court holds the stronger remedy, since a declaration names the right that the Act has breached

questions.onCorrect: A strike-down ends a statute's force, while a declaration only asks Parliament to act, so the two reports describe two different arrangements.

misconceptions.feedback: Not every democracy lets courts strike statutes down. The United Kingdom and the Netherlands do not, and a declaration of incompatibility is the most a British court can offer.
A declaration does not disapply the Act. It works as a request to Parliament, so the court holds less power over the statute than a court that can strike it down.

questions.prompt: The extract is Hamilton's reasoning about a statute that goes against a constitution. A town council, whose powers come from the state's charter, passes a rule that the charter forbids. Following his reasoning, what is the rule?

extracts.text: No legislative act, therefore, contrary to the Constitution, can be valid. To deny this, would be to affirm, that the deputy is greater than his principal; that the servant is above his master; that the representatives of the people are superior to the people themselves
extracts.who: Alexander Hamilton, The Federalist No. 78
extracts.when: published under the name Publius in McLean's edition on 28 May 1788
extracts.kind: An essay written to persuade voters to ratify the Constitution of the United States

hints: In Hamilton's picture the council is an agent and the charter is the commission it was given. What does an agent's act that goes beyond the commission amount to?
Does Hamilton make the validity of such an act depend on who elected the agent?

acceptedIdeas: Void, since the council acted against what its creating authority allowed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Void, since the council acted against what its creating authority allowed

choices.label: Void, since the council acted against what its creating authority allowed
Valid, since the council was elected by the town and speaks for all of its voters
Valid until the state legislature votes to cancel it by passing a new statute

questions.onCorrect: An agent's act against the commission is void, so the council's rule fails for the same reason as a statute against the constitution.

misconceptions.feedback: Hamilton argues that the deputy cannot be greater than the principal and the servant cannot be above the master. An elected agent still acts only within what its commission allows.
The extract says an act contrary to the commission cannot be valid, which does not wait on a later vote. The rule is void from the start.

questions.prompt: A legislature angry at a run of rulings votes to cut every judge's salary. Source A is a clause of the United States Constitution and Source B a clause of the Australian one. What do the two clauses do to such a law?

extracts.text: The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good behavior, and shall, at stated Times, receive for their Services, a Compensation, which shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.
extracts.who: The Constitution of the United States, Article III, section 1
extracts.when: agreed at the Convention on 17 September 1787
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of the United States

extracts.text: shall receive such remuneration as the Parliament may fix; but the remuneration shall not be diminished during their continuance in office.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 72
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

hints: Read the end of each clause: what may happen to a judge's pay during the time they hold office?
Does the Australian clause let Parliament fix the pay and also cut it later?

acceptedIdeas: Block it in both countries, since each protects pay while a judge holds office
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Block it in both countries, since each protects pay while a judge holds office

choices.label: Block it in the United States only, since only the United States names good behaviour
Allow it in both countries, since a legislature fixes the pay for every public office, judges included
Block it in both countries, since each protects pay while a judge holds office

questions.onCorrect: Both clauses fix a judge's pay while in office, which is one of the protections that lets judges rule against the other branches.

misconceptions.feedback: The Australian clause also bars any reduction of pay during a justice's time in office. Good behaviour is a separate protection, concerned with removal.
Both clauses give the legislature a say in setting pay, and both forbid reducing it during a judge's time in office. A pay cut aimed at judges is the kind of pressure they exist to stop.

questions.prompt: Country T has set up one court whose only work is to decide whether statutes conform to the constitution. Other courts may ask it to look at a statute but may not rule on the question themselves. What is such a court called?
hints: Which of the three approaches gives the power to a single court and denies it to the others?
The name says what the court is for: the constitution is the thing it checks laws against.

acceptedIdeas: constitutional court
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: constitutional court

questions.onCorrect: A constitutional court does this work and no other, as in Austria and Germany.

misconceptions.feedback: A supreme court that also hears ordinary cases belongs to the second approach, where general courts review statutes. The court in Country T does this one job and no other.
General or ordinary courts hear every kind of case, and in Country T they cannot rule on a statute. Look for the name of the single court that can.

questions.prompt: A party that wins more votes than another can still end up with far fewer seats. What could make that happen?
hints: Think about how a country that elects one member for each district would count votes. Does a vote for a party that finishes second help it?
If a party's votes are spread thinly over many districts and it leads in few of them, what happens to its seats?

acceptedIdeas: Each seat goes to whoever leads in a district, so thinly spread votes can win few seats
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each seat goes to whoever leads in a district, so thinly spread votes can win few seats

choices.label: Seats are shared out in proportion to votes, so the smaller party must have lost votes in the count
Parties that have governed before are given extra seats, whatever their votes this time
Each seat goes to whoever leads in a district, so thinly spread votes can win few seats

questions.onCorrect: Under a district rule a party needs to lead somewhere to win a seat, so votes spread thinly can produce few seats however many there are in total.

misconceptions.feedback: If seats followed votes in proportion, a party with more votes could hardly end up with far fewer seats. The 2024 figures point to a rule that counts district by district.
None of the rules in this lesson gives seats for past success. Seats come from the votes cast, and the rule that turns votes into seats is what decides the result.

questions.prompt: In an invented country each district elects one member by plurality. Two parties each win 20 percent of the votes nationally. The first party's voters are packed into a handful of districts, and the second's are spread evenly over all of them. Which party is likely to win more seats?
hints: Under plurality, what does a party have to do in a district to win its seat?
Which party is more likely to come first somewhere: the one that packs its votes in a few districts, or the one that spreads them evenly?

acceptedIdeas: The first, since its votes come first in the districts where they are packed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first, since its votes come first in the districts where they are packed

choices.label: The first, since its votes come first in the districts where they are packed
The second, since having some support in every district adds to its seats in each one
Both the same, since equal shares of the vote give equal shares of the seats

questions.onCorrect: Plurality rewards finishing first in a district, so concentrated support turns into seats more readily than the same support spread thinly.

misconceptions.feedback: Support in every district helps only where it finishes first. A party that is a distant second everywhere wins no district at all.
That is what proportional rules aim for. Under plurality the seats come from district contests, so where the votes sit matters as much as how many there are.

questions.prompt: Eight seats are shared among three parties first by D'Hondt and then by largest remainder with the Hare quota, using the same votes. The smallest party wins no seat under one method and one seat under the other. Which method gives it the seat, and what does that suggest about the two methods?
hints: Recall which of the two methods the lesson said favours large parties.
A party with a big fractional remainder after the quota division can still win a seat. Which method works that way?

acceptedIdeas: Largest remainder, which suggests it is more generous to small parties
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Largest remainder, which suggests it is more generous to small parties

choices.label: D'Hondt, which suggests it is more generous to small parties
Largest remainder, which suggests it is more generous to small parties
Largest remainder, which suggests it is more generous to large parties

questions.onCorrect: Largest remainder with the Hare quota gave the smallest party a seat that D'Hondt withheld, which fits the articles' account of D'Hondt as favouring large parties.

misconceptions.feedback: D'Hondt gave the smallest party nothing in the example, and the article says it tilts towards large parties and coalitions.
Largest remainder gave the smallest party its seat. The article says the Hare quota is kinder to less popular parties than the Droop quota is.

questions.prompt: Two countries elect by single transferable vote with the Droop quota. In one, each district elects 5 members. In the other, each district elects 21. In which would you expect more parties to win seats?
hints: The Droop quota as a share of the vote is one over the number of seats plus one. What happens to that share as the number of seats rises?
A smaller share needed for a seat means the bar is lower. Does a lower bar let in more parties or fewer?

acceptedIdeas: In the 21-seat districts, since a much smaller share of the vote guarantees a seat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the 21-seat districts, since a much smaller share of the vote guarantees a seat

choices.label: In the 5-seat districts, since a small district makes it easier for small parties to win
In the 21-seat districts, since a much smaller share of the vote guarantees a seat
In both alike, since the Droop quota is applied in the same way to every district

questions.onCorrect: More seats in a district lower the share of the vote that guarantees one, which is why New South Wales sees seven or eight parties win and Malta two.

misconceptions.feedback: In a 5-seat district it takes about a sixth of the vote to be sure of a seat, which shuts out small parties. Malta's five-member districts keep a very strong two-party system.
The quota is calculated the same way, but its size depends on the seats: one over the seats plus one. A 21-seat district needs about a twenty-second of the vote, so more parties pass the bar.

questions.prompt: A newspaper says that Queensland's 2012 election, with a Gallagher index of 31.16, shows the voters there were cheated. What does the index itself show?
hints: The index is built from the difference between each party's share of the votes and its share of the seats. What kind of quantity is that?
Does the number describe one election, or every election the system will ever hold?

acceptedIdeas: The size of the gap between vote shares and seat shares in that election
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The size of the gap between vote shares and seat shares in that election

choices.label: The size of the gap between vote shares and seat shares in that election
The share of voters whose preferred party was treated unfairly
The extent to which Queensland's system always departs from proportionality

questions.onCorrect: The Gallagher index sums up how far seat shares sit from vote shares in one election, and it leaves the question of fairness open.

misconceptions.feedback: The index adds the gaps for all parties into one number. It does not say whose votes were treated unfairly, and it does not call any gap unfair.
The index describes a single election. It cannot show that the same system departs from proportionality to the same degree in every election.

questions.prompt: Source A is an argument made by supporters of first past the post, and Source B one made by supporters of proportional representation. What do they disagree about most sharply?

extracts.text: The ability of FPTP to manufacture majority governments has been cited by its supporters as an advantage over proportional representation systems. In the latter, smaller parties may act as 'kingmakers' in coalitions using their bargaining power and therefore, arguably, their influence on policy is more than proportional to their parliamentary size.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "First-past-the-post voting" (revision 1384228971, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

extracts.text: Supporters of PR see coalitions as an advantage, forcing compromise between parties to form a coalition at the centre of the political spectrum
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Proportional representation" (revision 1385633303, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Underline what each source says about coalitions. Does each treat them the same way?
Source A says a small party in a coalition can use its bargaining power. How does Source B describe the same bargaining?

acceptedIdeas: Whether the bargaining that coalitions need is a fault or an advantage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether the bargaining that coalitions need is a fault or an advantage

choices.label: Whether a party's share of the seats should match its share of the votes
Whether a party can govern alone without winning a majority of the votes
Whether the bargaining that coalitions need is a fault or an advantage

questions.onCorrect: Supporters of first past the post see coalition bargaining as giving small parties undue influence, and supporters of proportional representation see it as forcing compromise.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither extract mentions that match. Both are about coalitions, and they disagree over whether the bargaining coalitions need is a good thing.
Source A mentions majority governments, but neither extract says anything about whether a majority of votes is needed. The disagreement is about coalition bargaining.

questions.prompt: Source A gives each Original State the same number of senators, and Source B gives each at least five members of the House. Compared with a rule that follows population alone, which State do the two rules favour most?

extracts.text: Until the Parliament otherwise provides there shall be six senators for each Original State.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 7
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

extracts.text: But notwithstanding anything in this section, five members at least shall be chosen in each Original State.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 24
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

hints: Imagine a State with very few people. What does it get under each rule, and what would a population-only rule have given it?
A minimum matters only to a State that would otherwise fall below it. Which States are those?

acceptedIdeas: The least populous State, since six senators and five members are guaranteed to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The least populous State, since six senators and five members are guaranteed to it

choices.label: The most populous State, since it has the most people to count towards the quota
Every State alike, since each receives the same number of senators
The least populous State, since six senators and five members are guaranteed to it

questions.onCorrect: A fixed number of senators and a floor of five members raise the smallest States' shares above their shares of the people.

misconceptions.feedback: A rule that counts people gives the most populous State its largest share, and the two rules in the extracts are the ones that depart from counting people. A fixed number for every State helps the smallest most.
The same number of senators gives a small State a larger share of the Senate than of the people. It gives the larger States a smaller one, so the effect is not alike.

questions.prompt: In an invented country a Green party wins 9 percent of the votes, spread evenly over every district, and no seats under plurality. The country then moves to a single national list with seats shared by D'Hondt. What is likely to happen to the party's seats?
hints: Under plurality, the party's seats depend on district results. What do they depend on under a national list?
Which kind of party did the lesson say D'Hondt tends to favour, large or small?

acceptedIdeas: It wins some, since seats now follow votes across the whole country
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It wins some, since seats now follow votes across the whole country

choices.label: It wins some, since seats now follow votes across the whole country
It still wins none, since D'Hondt gives seats only to parties that finish first somewhere
It wins far more than its share, since D'Hondt favours the smallest parties

questions.onCorrect: A party whose support was spread evenly gains from a national count, because plurality penalised its spread and D'Hondt does not.

misconceptions.feedback: D'Hondt works on each party's national vote total, divided by one, two, three and so on. Finishing first in a district plays no part in it.
D'Hondt tends to favour large parties and coalitions over small parties. A party with 9 percent should get a share near that, and some rounding either way.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants one number that sums up how far an election's seat shares departed from its vote shares, across all the parties. Which measure from the lesson does she use?
hints: The measure squares the gap for each party, halves the sum and takes the square root.
It is named for the political scientist who proposed it, and a score of 5 or less was the Canadian committee's target.

acceptedIdeas: Gallagher index
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gallagher index

questions.onCorrect: The Gallagher index gives one number for the gap between votes and seats, with 0 meaning a perfectly proportional result.

misconceptions.feedback: A quota is a threshold in votes that earns a seat. The measure asked for compares vote shares with seat shares across all parties.
D'Hondt is a way of sharing out seats. The measure asked for describes how far a finished result is from proportional.

questions.prompt: A town of 400 settles every question at a meeting where each adult votes. A majority in the town shares an interest in taxing a minority. What in the town's own arrangement stands in the way?
hints: Ask what a majority needs, beyond its own votes, to get what it wants in this town.
Does anyone in the arrangement have the power to say no to a majority that votes together?

acceptedIdeas: Nothing in the arrangement, since the majority's vote settles every question
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing in the arrangement, since the majority's vote settles every question

choices.label: The minority's right to speak at the meeting before the vote is taken
The town's small size, since a majority of 400 would struggle to act together
Nothing in the arrangement, since the majority's vote settles every question

questions.onCorrect: A meeting where every adult votes puts no check on a majority with a shared interest, which is the weakness Madison finds in a society governed this way.

misconceptions.feedback: Speaking before the vote doesn't change its result. A majority that shares an interest only has to vote, and nothing in the meeting checks it.
Small size works the other way. Madison says a society like this makes it easy for people who share a motive to communicate and act together.

questions.prompt: A newspaper writes of 'the party's left-wing faction'. A history of 1787 uses 'faction' as Madison defined it. Do the two uses of the word mean the same?
hints: Which of the two uses describes a part of a party, and which describes any group of citizens?
Could a faction in Madison's sense be a majority of the whole? Could the newspaper's?

acceptedIdeas: No, since Madison's faction is any group, even a majority, acting against others' rights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since Madison's faction is any group, even a majority, acting against others' rights

choices.label: No, since Madison's faction is any group, even a majority, acting against others' rights
Yes, since in both a faction is a subgroup of a party that argues with its leaders
Yes, since in both a faction is a small group holding extreme views that others reject

questions.onCorrect: A faction in Madison's sense is judged by what it does to others, and a faction in the newspaper's sense by where it sits inside a party.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the newspaper's use means a subgroup of a party. Madison's definition covers any group of citizens drawn together by a shared passion or interest against the rights of others or the community's interests.
Madison's definition includes a majority, and neither use depends on extreme views. In his sense a group is a faction because of what it does to others.

questions.prompt: Country N is large and its people work in many trades, from farming to commerce to manufacturing. Town T has 400 citizens, nearly all farmers. According to Madison's argument, where is a majority more likely to share a motive to invade others' rights, and why?
hints: Which place has the greater variety of interests among its citizens?
