In Madison's argument, what does a wider sphere do to the chance that a majority shares one motive?

acceptedIdeas: In Town T, since a narrow community shares its interests and can act in unison
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In Town T, since a narrow community shares its interests and can act in unison

choices.label: In Country N, since a larger population gives a majority more numbers to act with
In Town T, since a narrow community shares its interests and can act in unison
In both alike, since a majority forms around the same interests in any society

questions.onCorrect: A wide sphere takes in many interests, so a majority with one motive is less likely, which is why Madison prefers a large republic.

misconceptions.feedback: Madison argues the reverse. A larger sphere takes in a greater variety of interests, which makes a common motive less probable.
For Madison size matters. The wider the sphere, the more varied the interests, and the harder it is for people who share a motive to find their strength and act together.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson's distinctions, what is each of these six invented organisations?
hints: Ask what each organisation is for: electing candidates, pressing a policy, or pulling a party in one direction.
A group inside a party shares its label, and an interest group stays outside the contest for seats.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nominating organisation and the movement that puts up candidates are parties. The trade association and the river campaign are interest groups. The legislators pressing for a stricter budget and the bloc against the health plan are factions inside a party.

questions.onCorrect: Each description is placed by its aim: electing candidates, advancing a policy, or pulling a party one way.

items.label: An organisation that nominates candidates under one label and tries to form a government
items.explanation: It is focused on electing candidates and taking part in governing, which is what makes it a party.

items.label: A trade association that lobbies for lower import duties and endorses no candidate
items.explanation: It tries to influence policy and puts up no one for office, so it is an interest group.

items.label: A group of legislators inside a party who press its leaders to adopt a stricter budget
items.explanation: It is a subgroup within a party, which is the meaning of faction in the party article.

items.label: A campaign for cleaner rivers that publishes reports and meets ministers but puts up no candidates
items.explanation: Its aim is a policy, and it works by influencing those who govern, so it is an interest group.

items.label: A bloc inside a governing party that votes together against the leadership's plan on health
items.explanation: It sits within a party and pulls it one way, which makes it a faction inside the party.

items.label: A movement that registers voters and puts up candidates for the national legislature in most districts
items.explanation: It puts up candidates to win seats, which is the aim of a party.

questions.prompt: An association campaigning for better farming standards wins a rule that helps every farmer. Why might it find it harder to recruit members afterwards?
hints: Who gets the benefit of the new rule: only the members, or every farmer?
If you would receive the benefit whether or not you joined, what would joining add for you?

acceptedIdeas: Non-members get the benefit anyway, so many farmers have little reason to join
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Non-members get the benefit anyway, so many farmers have little reason to join

choices.label: Members lose part of the benefit when others join, so they discourage new recruits
Non-members get the benefit anyway, so many farmers have little reason to join
A group that has won its rule has finished its aim, so its members leave

questions.onCorrect: A benefit that reaches non-members gives people little reason to pay for membership, which is the free rider problem.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the case makes the benefit shrink when more farmers join. The problem is that the rule helps farmers who never joined.
The free rider problem is about recruiting. When the benefit reaches non-members too, joining adds little for the individual farmer.

questions.prompt: In a large republic one party wins a majority in the legislature election after election and uses it to burden a minority. A critic says this refutes Madison's argument about the large republic. What does his argument claim?
hints: Look at how strong Madison's wording is: less probable, or impossible?
Does he think the causes of faction can be removed?

acceptedIdeas: That a common-motive majority is less probable and harder to unite, though still possible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a common-motive majority is less probable and harder to unite, though still possible

choices.label: That a large republic removes the causes of faction, so no such majority could ever form
That representatives chosen by the voters will always protect a minority from the majority
That a common-motive majority is less probable and harder to unite, though still possible

questions.onCorrect: Madison's claim is about probability and about controlling effects, so one majority that forms in spite of the wide sphere doesn't refute it.

misconceptions.feedback: Madison holds that nothing can remove what causes faction. His claim is about controlling its effects.
The passage says a wide sphere makes a common motive less probable, which falls short of always. It offers a cure for the mischief and no guarantee.

questions.prompt: A political scientist notes that elections held in single-member districts under a plurality rule tend to produce two-party systems. By what name is this observation known?
hints: The observation is named for the person who first made it, in the 1950s.
It links an electoral rule to the number of parties, a link the last lesson began to explore.

acceptedIdeas: Duverger's law
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Duverger's law

questions.onCorrect: Duverger's observation links an electoral rule to a party system, though whether it holds has been heavily debated.

misconceptions.feedback: That names a different idea. The observation about plurality and two parties carries the name of the political scientist who made it in the 1950s.
Madison wrote about faction in 1787. The observation about plurality elections and two-party systems was made in the 1950s by another writer.

questions.prompt: Madison separates a pure democracy from a republic. Which of these governments would he call a republic?
hints: Madison names two differences from a pure democracy: who runs the government, and how large the society can be.
In a republic, who chooses the few who govern?

acceptedIdeas: A country of millions whose citizens choose a small body to make the laws
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A country of millions whose citizens choose a small body to make the laws

choices.label: A village of 300 whose adults assemble to vote on every law themselves
A country of millions whose citizens choose a small body to make the laws
A country of millions where nobles make the laws and name their own successors

questions.onCorrect: A republic in Madison's sense is a government of representatives elected by the rest, which can cover many citizens and a wide territory.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Madison's pure democracy, where citizens assemble and run the government in person.
A republic in his sense hands the government to a few citizens elected by the rest. Nobles who name their own successors aren't chosen by the citizens.

questions.prompt: The extract separates four kinds of organisation. A farmers' union lobbies for subsidies and backs candidates of two parties, but puts up none of its own. How would you classify it?

extracts.text: a party is focused on electing candidates, whereas a parliamentary group is a group of political parties, a political faction is a subgroup within a political party, and an advocacy group is focused on advancing a policy agenda.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Political party" (revision 1384438036, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Does the union put up its own candidates, or does it press for a policy?
Which of the four kinds in the extract is defined by its focus on a policy agenda?

acceptedIdeas: As an advocacy group, since its focus is advancing a policy agenda
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As an advocacy group, since its focus is advancing a policy agenda

choices.label: As an advocacy group, since its focus is advancing a policy agenda
As a party, since backing candidates is part of taking part in elections
As a faction, since it works inside both of the parties it backs

questions.onCorrect: The union's focus is policy, so it is an advocacy group, whichever candidates it happens to back.

misconceptions.feedback: A party is focused on electing candidates of its own, and this union puts up none.
A faction is a subgroup within a party. The union is an outside organisation and is part of neither party.

questions.prompt: A poll asks people whether they support a trade law that most of them have never heard of, and a majority say yes. What does the result most likely show?
hints: Think about what a person who has never heard of a law can say when a pollster asks about it.
People who are asked about something they know little about may answer for a reason other than their own view. What might that reason be?

acceptedIdeas: Many answers are given to please the pollster and reflect no view already held
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many answers are given to please the pollster and reflect no view already held

choices.label: A majority has studied the law closely and approves of what it does
Surveys are worthless, since they can never measure what any group of people thinks
Many answers are given to please the pollster and reflect no view already held

questions.onCorrect: People asked about a subject they know little about often give an answer meant to please, which the article calls a pseudo-opinion.

misconceptions.feedback: Most respondents had never heard of the law, so a majority cannot have studied it. A yes from someone who knows nothing about a law shows little about what they think of it.
The article says public opinion can be obtained accurately through survey sampling. The trouble here lies with the question, which asks about something most respondents know nothing about.

questions.prompt: Two newspapers report the same transport plan. One calls it 'a new tax on drivers' and the other 'a charge that pays to repair the roads'. What is the difference an example of?
hints: Both papers cover the plan, so the difference lies in something other than whether it is reported.
Which word describes presenting the same story in a particular way to push the reader's attitude?

acceptedIdeas: Framing, since each presents the story in a way meant to sway readers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Framing, since each presents the story in a way meant to sway readers

choices.label: Framing, since each presents the story in a way meant to sway readers
Agenda setting, since each decides whether the plan is newsworthy
A pseudo-opinion, since each reports what it thinks readers want to hear

questions.onCorrect: Framing presents a story in a particular way to sway the audience, so the same plan can look like a tax or like a repair charge.

misconceptions.feedback: Agenda setting concerns which stories are reported and when. Both papers report this plan, and they differ in how they describe it.
A pseudo-opinion is an answer that a person gives to please a questioner about something they know little about. Neither paper is answering a question.

questions.prompt: A city floods repeatedly, and over several years these five events happen. Put them in the order of the policy cycle.
hints: Start with the event in which the problem comes to the government's attention, and end with the one that asks whether the policy worked.
Approval comes after a plan exists and before anyone builds anything.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pressure on the council puts flooding on the agenda, officials formulate a plan, the council's vote legitimates it, the agency implements it, and the auditors evaluate the result.

questions.onCorrect: Each event is one stage of the cycle in order: agenda setting, formulation, legitimation, implementation and evaluation, and the evaluation could send flooding back to the agenda.

items: Residents and newspapers press the council to treat flooding as a problem
Officials draft a plan that sets out options and their costs
The council votes to approve the plan and its funding
A new agency builds the flood barriers
Auditors measure whether flooding has fallen

questions.prompt: In one year a government spends more than it collects in receipts. What is such a budget called, and how is the gap usually financed?
hints: Compare the two sides of the budget: which one is larger?
If spending is larger than receipts, where does the money for the difference have to come from?

acceptedIdeas: A deficit budget, financed mostly by borrowing from private lenders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A deficit budget, financed mostly by borrowing from private lenders

choices.label: A surplus budget, financed mostly by taxes collected in earlier years
A deficit budget, financed mostly by borrowing from private lenders
A balanced budget, financed mostly by receipts expected in the following year

questions.onCorrect: Spending above receipts is a deficit, and governments usually finance it by borrowing from lenders at home or abroad or from international institutions.

misconceptions.feedback: A surplus is the reverse: receipts exceed spending. Spending above receipts leaves a gap that has to be covered with money from somewhere else.
A balanced budget has receipts equal to spending, so there is no gap to finance. Here spending is larger than receipts.

questions.prompt: A parliament passes a law to cut hospital waiting times. Two years later waits are unchanged, because the new agency set up to carry out the law has no staff. Which stage of the cycle failed?
hints: The law passed, so which stages came before it and are finished?
Which stage covers setting up the organisation that carries a policy out and giving it what it needs?

acceptedIdeas: Implementation, since the agency lacked the resources to carry the policy out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Implementation, since the agency lacked the resources to carry the policy out

choices.label: Legitimation, since the law needed more approval before it could take any effect
Agenda setting, since waiting times had not been recognised as a problem at all
Implementation, since the agency lacked the resources to carry the policy out

questions.onCorrect: Implementation includes giving the responsible organisation the resources to act, so an unstaffed agency is a failure at that stage.

misconceptions.feedback: The law was passed, so approval was gathered. What failed came afterwards, when the agency could not do what the law asked.
Parliament passed a law on waiting times, so the problem was on the agenda. The failure is that the law did not turn into action.

questions.prompt: A parliament approves a plan to set up a flood agency, and the finance ministry publishes a budget that lists the plan's cost. A year later the agency still cannot hire anyone. What is missing?
hints: Both constitutions in the lesson say no money leaves the Treasury without something. Without what?
Does a published budget by itself authorise the spending it lists?

acceptedIdeas: An appropriation made by law, since a budget alone doesn't release any money
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An appropriation made by law, since a budget alone doesn't release any money

choices.label: An appropriation made by law, since a budget alone doesn't release any money
A balanced budget, since a deficit stops any agency from being paid at all
A place on the agenda, since parliament never recognised the flood problem

questions.onCorrect: A budget projects revenue and spending but doesn't itself appropriate funds, so a further law is needed before an agency can spend.

misconceptions.feedback: A government can run a deficit and still pay its agencies, financing the gap by borrowing. What a budget cannot do alone is authorise the money.
Parliament approved a plan, so the problem was on the agenda long before. What the story lacks is the step that releases the money.

questions.prompt: A city's plan to ban cars from its centre is put to a referendum and passes. Which stage of the policy cycle is the referendum?
hints: This stage gathers approval for a policy, from an executive, a legislature or the public.
A referendum is one way of seeking consent. Which stage is about consent?

acceptedIdeas: legitimation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: legitimation

questions.onCorrect: A referendum gathers approval for a policy, which is the stage of legitimation.

misconceptions.feedback: Agenda setting is the stage where a problem gets attention. The plan already exists, and the vote is about approving it.
Implementation is about carrying a policy out. The referendum happens before anything is built or enforced.
Formulation sets out options and costs. A referendum decides between a plan that has been drawn up and no plan.
Evaluation looks back at whether a policy worked. The referendum comes before the policy exists.

questions.prompt: A country introduces free school lunches, and over the following years polls show growing support for them. Which reading of the extract fits what happened?

extracts.text: social policy impacts public opinion. The goods and services the public gets via social policy builds normative expectations that shape public opinion.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Public opinion" (revision 1379833294, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: The extract names what social policy does to public opinion. Which way does the influence run?
Can you tell from the polls alone whether the support came before the lunches or after them?

acceptedIdeas: Policy can shape opinion, so some of the support may follow from the lunches themselves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Policy can shape opinion, so some of the support may follow from the lunches themselves

choices.label: Opinion alone shapes policy, so the polls show that voters wanted the lunches first
Policy can shape opinion, so some of the support may follow from the lunches themselves
Polls taken after a policy has started are worthless, since people answer to please

questions.onCorrect: Social policy builds expectations that shape opinion, so rising support after a policy begins may partly be an effect of it.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says what the public gets from social policy builds expectations that shape opinion, so influence can run from policy to opinion as well.
The extract doesn't say that. It describes a way policy shapes what people expect, and growing support after a policy is a pattern that fits that account.

questions.prompt: An economist designs a budget that puts every pound where it does most economic good, and the government's actual budget differs. Using the extract, what is the best explanation?

extracts.text: Government budgets also have a political basis wherein different interests push and pull in an attempt to obtain benefits and avoid burdens.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Government budget" (revision 1374476545, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: The extract says a government budget has more than one basis. Which basis explains the difference from the economist's design?
Think of who gains and who loses from each line of a budget. Would they all accept the economist's design?

acceptedIdeas: Budgets are also political, as interests press to gain benefits and avoid burdens
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Budgets are also political, as interests press to gain benefits and avoid burdens

choices.label: Budgets are also political, as interests press to gain benefits and avoid burdens
Constitutions bar governments from using the economist's method of allocating money
A budget is only a projection, so it needn't follow any method of allocation

questions.onCorrect: A government budget is shaped by competing interests as well as by economics, which is why it rarely matches a pure economic design.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says nothing about a ban. It says a government budget has a political basis as well as an economic one.
A budget is a projection, but the extract's point is about why its contents differ from a pure economic design: different interests push and pull.

questions.prompt: A town's voters, in a fair election and by a large majority, ban a small political group from meeting in the town hall. Does the size of the majority settle whether the ban is justified?
hints: Ask whether the group that lost the vote has any way to protect itself from the winners.
Think of the majority as a power, like a monarch's, and ask what a power can be used for.

acceptedIdeas: No, because even a large majority can use its power against a smaller group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because even a large majority can use its power against a smaller group

choices.label: Yes, because a law that most voters chose is justified by that choice and nothing more
No, because even a large majority can use its power against a smaller group
No, because a town may never ban any group from using any public building

questions.onCorrect: Mill and Tocqueville, the two writers in this lesson, both treat a majority as a power that can be turned against the people who lost the vote.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the vote as the whole test. A vote shows what most people want, and it leaves open whether what they want wrongs the group that lost.
A town can limit some conduct, and Mill's own principle allows it where the conduct harms others. What the option misses is that the size of a majority is not by itself a reason to ban anything.

questions.prompt: Here are six invented laws. Does Mill's principle, as the extract states it, allow the state to make each one?

extracts.text: the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.
extracts.who: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859)
extracts.when: published in 1859
extracts.kind: An essay on the relation between authority and liberty

hints: Ask of each law whether anyone other than the person it restricts is harmed.
Three of the laws are justified by the good of the person they restrict, or by what the majority dislikes. Mill's principle gives the state no warrant for those.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Allowed: the fine for loud music at three in the morning, the red-light law and the open-gate offence. Not allowed: the ban on food the council thinks unhealthy, the ban on a newspaper the council thinks foolish and the punishment of a habit that affects no one else.

questions.onCorrect: Each law is placed by one question: does it prevent harm to someone else, or does it limit a person for his own good or because others disapprove?

items.label: A town fines residents who play loud music at three in the morning
items.explanation: The noise harms the neighbours who are woken, so the law prevents harm to others.

items.label: A law forbids adults to eat food the council thinks unhealthy, though it harms no one else
items.explanation: It rests on the eater's own good, which Mill says is not a sufficient warrant.

items.label: A law forbids adults to read a newspaper the council thinks foolish, for their own improvement
items.explanation: Improving the reader is the reader's own good, and Mill allows only reasoning and persuasion for that.

items.label: A law requires drivers to stop at red lights
items.explanation: A driver who ignores the light can harm other people, so the law prevents harm to others.

items.label: A law makes it an offence to leave a gate open so that cattle enter a neighbour's crops
items.explanation: The cattle damage the neighbour's crops, which is harm to someone else.

items.label: A law punishes a habit the majority finds distasteful, though it affects no one else
items.explanation: What the majority dislikes is not harm to others, and other people's opinions are not a warrant to compel.

questions.prompt: A legislature elected by 60 percent of the voters bans the newspaper of the party that won the other 40 percent, and its supporters say the people have spoken. Which point in the extract answers them?

extracts.text: A majority taken collectively may be regarded as a being whose opinions, and most frequently whose interests, are opposed to those of another being, which is styled a minority. If it be admitted that a man, possessing absolute power, may misuse that power by wronging his adversaries, why should a majority not be liable to the same reproach?
extracts.who: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, volume 1 (Reeve translation)
extracts.when: published in 1835, after nine months in the United States in 1831 and 1832
extracts.kind: A French study of American society and democracy

hints: Find the sentence that compares a majority with a man who holds absolute power.
The supporters rely on the size of the majority. Does the extract treat size as the thing that makes a majority safe?

acceptedIdeas: A majority has opponents it can wrong, as a monarch can wrong his adversaries
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A majority has opponents it can wrong, as a monarch can wrong his adversaries

choices.label: A majority has opponents it can wrong, as a monarch can wrong his adversaries
A majority cannot wrong anyone, since authority begins in the will of the majority
A majority is dangerous only when it wins an election by a narrow margin

questions.onCorrect: The comparison treats the majority like any holder of power: it has opponents, and what it does to them is a separate question from how many voted for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The source of authority doesn't settle how it is used. Tocqueville asks why a majority should escape the reproach that applies to a man with absolute power who wrongs his adversaries.
The extract doesn't mention margins. The comparison applies to a majority as such, which he describes as having opinions and interests opposed to the minority's.

questions.prompt: A town has no law about what residents may say of the mayor. A shopkeeper who criticised the mayor in a letter is now ignored by customers, left off neighbours' invitations and dropped by friends, and has stopped speaking up. What is this, in Mill's terms?
hints: Who is pressing on the shopkeeper: an official, or the people around her?
Does the case need a law or an official to explain why she stopped speaking up?

acceptedIdeas: Social tyranny, since opinion applies the pressure and no law is needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Social tyranny, since opinion applies the pressure and no law is needed

choices.label: Tyranny of the magistrate, since the mayor's office is what was criticised
No tyranny at all, since no law was passed and no official imposed a penalty
Social tyranny, since opinion applies the pressure and no law is needed

questions.onCorrect: Mill describes a tyranny that leaves fewer ways to escape than many political ones, since it works through the opinion of the people around a person.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the case has a public authority acting against her. The pressure comes from customers, neighbours and friends, which Mill separates from the tyranny of the magistrate.
Mill's principle names the moral coercion of public opinion alongside legal penalties, so a coercion that uses no law can still be a tyranny.

questions.prompt: A private newspaper refuses to print a reader's letter, and the reader says this breaks the clause in the extract. Going by the wording of the clause, whom does it restrain?

extracts.text: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
extracts.who: The proposed Bill of Rights of the United States (twelve articles, text of 1789)
extracts.when: proposed in 1789
extracts.kind: A set of proposed amendments to the Constitution of the United States

hints: Find the actor the clause names, the one that is told what it shall not do.
Separate who holds a freedom from who is forbidden to interfere with it.

acceptedIdeas: Congress, the body the clause names as the maker of laws, and no one else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Congress, the body the clause names as the maker of laws, and no one else

choices.label: Congress, the body the clause names as the maker of laws, and no one else
Newspapers, since the clause names the press among the freedoms it lists
Every person and group equally, since the clause protects a right of the people

questions.onCorrect: A rights clause is read for the actor it names, and this one names the lawmaker, so it restrains Congress and says nothing of private owners.

misconceptions.feedback: The clause lists the press among the freedoms Congress may not abridge. It doesn't give the press any duty.

The clause names its target, which is Congress. It mentions a right of the people, but the restraint falls on the lawmaker. Whether other rules reach private groups is a separate question that this text doesn't answer.

questions.prompt: A constitution lets the government suspend some rights in a state of emergency. After a week of peaceful protests the government declares one and jails the organisers. What does the extract say about decrees of this kind?

extracts.text: Many constitutions allow the declaration under exceptional circumstances of some form of state of emergency during which some rights and guarantees are suspended. This provision can be and has been abused to allow a government to suppress dissent without regard for human rights
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Constitution" (revision 1383141919, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Look for what the extract says about how the provision has actually been used.
The extract says 'many constitutions'. Does it say that only some kinds of country have such a provision?

acceptedIdeas: The power to suspend rights can be abused, and has been, to suppress dissent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The power to suspend rights can be abused, and has been, to suppress dissent

choices.label: Any suspension of rights in an emergency is abuse, whatever the circumstances
The power to suspend rights can be abused, and has been, to suppress dissent
Only dictatorships write emergency provisions into their constitutions

questions.onCorrect: The extract names a risk in the provision itself: a government can use it to suppress dissent and disregard human rights.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract says many constitutions allow some rights to be suspended, and the article on civil liberties calls the extent of suspension a matter of debate. It names abuse as a risk without saying every suspension is one.
The extract says many constitutions contain such a provision. What it warns about is how the provision can be used.

questions.prompt: A town council bans a street rally because passers-by find its slogans deeply offensive, though nobody is struck or blocked. What does the principle in the extract settle about this ban?

extracts.text: That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.
extracts.who: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859)
extracts.when: published in 1859
extracts.kind: An essay on the relation between authority and liberty

hints: Does the extract define harm, or does it only say what harm is needed for?
Could two people who both accept the principle give different answers about this rally?

acceptedIdeas: It says the council needs a harm to others as its ground, but not whether offence is one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It says the council needs a harm to others as its ground, but not whether offence is one

choices.label: It says the council needs a harm to others as its ground, but not whether offence is one
It settles the case for the council, since offence to others is a harm and the ban prevents it
It settles the case for the rally, since slogans concern only the people who shout them

questions.onCorrect: The principle fixes the kind of reason a law needs. What counts as harm is a further question, and people who accept the principle can answer it differently.

misconceptions.feedback: The principle doesn't say that offence is a harm. It names harm to others as the ground, and whether offence counts is the point on which people applying it can disagree.
Other people hear slogans, so the principle doesn't put them out of reach. Whether hearing them counts as harm is what the principle leaves open.

questions.prompt: These are two extracts, one from Mill and one from Tocqueville. What do both claim?

extracts.text: it practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since, though not usually upheld by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself.
extracts.who: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859)
extracts.when: published in 1859
extracts.kind: An essay on the relation between authority and liberty

extracts.text: the majority possesses a power which is physical and moral at the same time; it acts upon the will as well as upon the actions of men, and it represses not only all contest, but all controversy.
extracts.who: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, volume 1 (Reeve translation)
extracts.when: published in 1835, after nine months in the United States in 1831 and 1832
extracts.kind: A French study of American society and democracy

hints: Find in each extract what the majority or society acts on.
One extract names the will and the other names the soul. Is a law needed to reach either?

acceptedIdeas: That a majority can reach people's minds as well as their actions, with no law
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a majority can reach people's minds as well as their actions, with no law

choices.label: That a majority can reach people's minds as well as their actions, with no law
That the main way a majority oppresses a minority is through legal penalties
That every majority will misuse its power sooner or later, whatever its laws

questions.onCorrect: Mill and Tocqueville stress different things, but both say a majority's power reaches people's minds, which is why a law is not the only thing to watch.

misconceptions.feedback: Mill says the social tyranny he describes is not usually upheld by extreme penalties, and Tocqueville says the majority acts on the will as well as the actions. Both place the danger beyond penalties.
Neither extract says that. Tocqueville, in the passage on abuses, says he does not claim they occur frequently.

questions.prompt: In a country with no legal protection for minorities, the majority has so far treated them gently, and a commentator says this shows minorities are safe there. What would Tocqueville reply, going by the extract?

extracts.text: I do not say that tyrannical abuses frequently occur in America at the present day, but I maintain that no sure barrier is established against them, and that the causes which mitigate the government are to be found in the circumstances and the manners of the country more than in its laws.
extracts.who: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, volume 1 (Reeve translation)
extracts.when: published in 1835, after nine months in the United States in 1831 and 1832
extracts.kind: A French study of American society and democracy

hints: Find what the extract says the mildness of the government owes its existence to.
Does Tocqueville claim abuses are common, or only that nothing reliable stands against them?

acceptedIdeas: That gentleness so far rests on circumstances and manners, so it is no sure barrier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That gentleness so far rests on circumstances and manners, so it is no sure barrier

choices.label: That the majority will soon turn harsh, since abuses are frequent in every democracy
That gentleness shows the laws are working, since they have protected the minority
That gentleness so far rests on circumstances and manners, so it is no sure barrier

questions.onCorrect: A mildness that rests on circumstances and manners lasts only as long as they do, which is why Tocqueville wants a barrier more dependable than that.

misconceptions.feedback: He says the opposite about frequency: he does not say that abuses frequently occur. His claim is that nothing sure stands against them.
He attributes the mildness to the circumstances and manners of the country more than to its laws, so he doesn't credit the laws.

questions.prompt: In a company town no law requires anyone to attend the founder's church. But people who stay away are refused work, left off invitations and turned away by the shops. What name does Mill give to this kind of tyranny?
hints: Ask who exerts the pressure here, officials or society as a whole.
Mill adds this kind of tyranny to the tyranny of the magistrate.

acceptedIdeas: social tyranny
acceptedAlternatives: tyranny of prevailing opinion and feeling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: social tyranny

questions.onCorrect: Mill's social tyranny works through opinion and feeling, so a town can practise it with no law at all.

misconceptions.feedback: Tyranny of the magistrate works through public authorities. In this town no official acts, and the pressure comes from the people around the person, which is the further danger Mill adds to the first.

questions.prompt: Country P and country Q each have an elected regional assembly. In P the national parliament created the assembly by an ordinary law. In Q the assembly is named in the written constitution, which can't be changed without the regions' consent. In which country could the national government take powers from the assembly by itself?
hints: Ask what kind of text each assembly's powers rest on.
In which country does the national government need the regions' agreement before it changes the arrangement?

acceptedIdeas: Country P, because the parliament that made the law can change it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Country P, because the parliament that made the law can change it

choices.label: Country P, because the parliament that made the law can change it
Country Q, because a national government outranks every region
Neither, because an elected assembly keeps whatever powers it has been given

questions.onCorrect: P's division rests on a law the national parliament controls, which marks a unitary state. Q's rests on a constitution that needs both levels' consent, which marks a federation.

misconceptions.feedback: In Q the constitution names the assembly and can't be changed without the regions' consent, so the national government can't act alone. Outranking a region in everyday affairs is different from being able to rewrite the arrangement.
Being elected doesn't protect an assembly's powers. In P they come from an ordinary law, which the parliament that passed it can alter.

questions.prompt: A commentator says that because Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved power, the United Kingdom is a federation. Going by the extract, what is wrong with that claim?

extracts.text: The United Kingdom is an example of a unitary state. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have a degree of autonomous devolved power, but such power is delegated by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, which can enact laws unilaterally altering devolution.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Unitary state" (revision 1382822740, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Find who the extract says delegates the power to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Ask whether that body needs anyone's consent to change what it delegated.

acceptedIdeas: Their power is delegated by the UK Parliament, which can change it by its own law
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their power is delegated by the UK Parliament, which can change it by its own law

choices.label: Their power is delegated by the UK Parliament, which can change it by its own law
Devolved power covers too little, since a federation's regions must hold most powers
The extract is silent on who can change devolved power, so nothing can be judged

questions.onCorrect: Devolution is real power that the centre chose to hand over and can alter. A federation's regional powers don't depend on the centre's continuing choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Size isn't the test. A federation is marked by who can change the division, and the extract says the UK Parliament can alter devolution unilaterally.
The extract does say: the Parliament of the United Kingdom delegates the power and can change it by laws of its own.

questions.prompt: A student says that most countries must be federations, since the United States, Brazil, India, Germany and Australia all are. Going by the extract, what is wrong with that reasoning?

extracts.text: A large majority of the UN member countries, 166 out of 193, have a unitary system of government, while significant population and land mass is under some kind of federation.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Unitary state" (revision 1382822740, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Does naming five examples tell you how many states in all are federal?
Read the count in the extract: how many of the 193 are unitary, and how many are left?

acceptedIdeas: Naming federations doesn't count them all, and 166 of the 193 UN members are unitary
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Naming federations doesn't count them all, and 166 of the 193 UN members are unitary

choices.label: Naming federations doesn't count them all, and 166 of the 193 UN members are unitary
Those five countries are not federations, because each has a unitary system of government
Federations are so rare that they hold little of the world's people or land

questions.onCorrect: Most UN members, 166 of 193, are unitary, and federations still hold a significant share of the world's people and land, since counting states and counting people give different pictures.

misconceptions.feedback: All five are on Wikipedia's list of federations today. The extract's point is about the count, and the count shows that unitary states are the large majority.
The extract says that a significant share of the world's population and land lies under federations. They are a minority of states and still cover a large part of the world.

questions.prompt: A new kind of activity appears that none of these five constitutions mentions. Going by the rule each one follows for powers it doesn't list, which level holds the power to make laws about it?
hints: Ask first whether the constitution lists the federal government's powers or the regions' powers.
Where the list belongs to the federal government, the rest goes to the regions, and where the list belongs to the regions, the rest goes to the centre.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: States or provinces: the United States, Germany and Australia. The central government: Canada and India.

questions.onCorrect: The rule for unlisted powers is a choice each constitution makes, so it has to be learned country by country and can't be read off the word federal.

items.label: United States
items.explanation: The proposed twelfth article reserves powers not delegated to the United States to the States or to the people.

items.label: Germany
items.explanation: Wikipedia says the German constitution keeps with the states whatever it doesn't specifically give to the federal government.

items.label: Australia
items.explanation: The Commonwealth's powers are the ones listed, and the States keep every other area of responsibility.

items.label: Canada
items.explanation: Wikipedia says Canada's constitution leaves with the federal government the powers it doesn't explicitly grant to the provinces.

items.label: India
items.explanation: Wikipedia says the same of India: powers not explicitly granted to the states stay with the federal government.

questions.prompt: Australia's Commonwealth Parliament passes a law about currency, a matter on the Commonwealth's list. A State parliament, elected more recently, passes a law that contradicts it. Which law prevails?

extracts.text: When a law of a State is inconsistent with a law of the Commonwealth, the latter shall prevail, and the former shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be invalid.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 109
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

hints: Find the sentence that says what happens when a State law is inconsistent with a Commonwealth law.
Does the extract say anything about which law came later, or about who was elected more recently?

acceptedIdeas: The Commonwealth law, and the State law is invalid to the extent that it conflicts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Commonwealth law, and the State law is invalid to the extent that it conflicts

choices.label: The State law, since the States keep the powers that the Constitution doesn't list
The law passed later, since the more recent parliament reflects the voters' wishes
The Commonwealth law, and the State law is invalid to the extent that it conflicts

questions.onCorrect: Where the two levels conflict, section 109 gives priority to the Commonwealth law, however recent the State's law.

misconceptions.feedback: Currency is one of the Commonwealth's listed powers, so it isn't an unlisted matter, and section 109 settles a conflict in the Commonwealth law's favour.
Section 109 doesn't ask which law is later. It makes the State law invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.

questions.prompt: Yes carries three of the six states. Why doesn't that count as a majority of the states?
hints: A majority is more than half. How many is half of six?
Does the rule count the states or the voters in them?

acceptedIdeas: A majority needs more than half of all the states, and three is exactly half of six
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A majority needs more than half of all the states, and three is exactly half of six

choices.label: A majority needs more than half of all the states, and three is exactly half of six
The three states Yes lost hold more voters between them than the three it carried
Yes needed to carry every state, since the rule asks for majorities in the states

questions.onCorrect: A majority of six states is four, and a tie at three is not a majority.

misconceptions.feedback: The three it carried have more voters between them, and the number of voters doesn't matter here. The state count asks how many states Yes carried, whatever their size.
The rule asks for majorities in a majority of the states, so four of six would have been enough.

questions.prompt: Yes wins in four of the five states, but trails nationally with 1,890,000 votes against 2,290,000. Does the proposal pass, and why?

extracts.text: And if in a majority of the States a majority of the electors voting approve the proposed law, and if a majority of all the electors voting also approve the proposed law, it shall be presented to the Governor-General for the Queen's assent.
extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 128
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted
extracts.kind: The founding legal text of Australia

hints: Check each of the two counts separately, and write down whether Yes wins it.
Does the rule let a win in one count make up for a loss in the other?

acceptedIdeas: No, because it loses the national count, though it carries four of the five states
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because it loses the national count, though it carries four of the five states

choices.label: Yes, because it carries four of the five states, which is a majority of the states
No, because it loses the national count, though it carries four of the five states
Yes, because a national majority isn't needed once most of the states have agreed

questions.onCorrect: A double majority is two tests, and a proposal that wins one and loses the other fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Carrying the states is only one of the two counts. The rule also needs a majority of all the voters, and Yes has fewer votes than No.
The rule needs both. Section 128 asks for majorities in a majority of the States, and a majority among all the electors voting as well.

questions.prompt: Country M's constitution lists the powers of the national parliament and gives every other power to its provinces. The national parliament can amend the constitution by an ordinary vote of its own members, without asking the provinces. Going by the extract, is M federal?

extracts.text: In federations, the provincial/regional governments share powers with the central government as equal actors through a written constitution, to which the consent of both is required to make amendments. This means that the sub-national units have a right to existence and powers that cannot be unilaterally changed by the central government.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, "Unitary state" (revision 1382822740, CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.when: retrieved on 14 November 2026
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article that summarises other sources

hints: Find the sentence in the extract about who must consent to amendments.
In M, can the national parliament change the provinces' powers without their agreement?

acceptedIdeas: No, because the centre can change the division by itself, as in a unitary state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the centre can change the division by itself, as in a unitary state

choices.label: No, because the centre can change the division by itself, as in a unitary state
Yes, because the constitution gives the provinces every power that it doesn't list
Yes, because the provinces' powers are written into the constitution itself

questions.onCorrect: Federal and unitary are told apart by who can change the division. In M the centre can, so the provinces hold their powers at its discretion.

misconceptions.feedback: Who keeps unlisted powers is something federations settle in different ways. It doesn't decide whether a state is federal, which depends on whether the centre alone can change the division.
A written text isn't enough. In a federation the constitution needs the consent of both levels to amend, and in M the centre alone can amend it.

questions.prompt: These are two extracts, one from the United States Constitution and one from Australia's. What do the two rules have in common?

extracts.who: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, section 128
extracts.when: an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament, text as enacted

hints: Find who in each extract has the last word before the change takes effect.

acceptedIdeas: Each needs approval from the states as well as from the national legislature
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each needs approval from the states as well as from the national legislature

choices.label: Each needs approval from the states as well as from the national legislature
Each puts the change to one vote of all the electors of the whole country
Each lets the national legislature finish an amendment it has proposed

questions.onCorrect: In both federations the states take part in the final decision, so the centre can't amend the division of powers on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: The United States text gives the vote to the legislatures or conventions of three fourths of the States, and Australia's asks for majorities in the States as well as nationally.
